title: Automating administration with the Dynatrace Managed Cluster API
summary:
Creating an environment for a new subsidiary, adding a user group, generating a token for the deployment pipeline, checking node status before maintenance: taken one at a time, these tasks take a few clicks in the Cluster Management Console. Repeated every week, across several clusters, by several administrators, they become a source of errors and configuration drift, unless you hand them over to the Dynatrace Managed Cluster API.

The Cluster API is built for exactly that. Separate from the environment API (https://{your-domain}/e/{environment-id}/api/…), it works at platform level: https://{your-domain}/api/cluster/v2/… for v2, and mostly https://{your-domain}/api/v1.0/onpremise/… for v1. It has no equivalent for a SaaS customer, because it is the cluster operator — you — who needs it.

This article covers what it can do, how to secure it, and offers concrete scripts to start serious automation.

Dynatrace Managed Cluster API or environment API?

Criterion Cluster API Environment API
Base URL https://{your-domain}/api/cluster/v2 and …/api/v1.0/onpremise (v1) `https://{your-domain}/e/{id}/api/v1
Token Cluster token (CMC, Settings > API tokens) Environment token
Scope Nodes, environments, users, groups, licences, cluster settings Entities, metrics, problems, monitoring settings, OneAgent deployment
Typical users Platform team Ops teams, CI/CD, third-party tools

Full automation often uses both: the Cluster API creates the environment and a first environment token, then the environment API takes over for monitoring configuration.

What is commonly automated

  • Environment lifecycle: creation, renaming, enabling/disabling, quotas (host units, sessions, storage).
  • Tokens: generating environment tokens to bootstrap tools.
  • Users and groups: creating groups, assigning permissions, audit exports (see the Managed access model).
  • Cluster status: list of nodes, state, version; useful before and after maintenance.
  • Settings: SMTP, proxy, backup, depending on what your version exposes.

The exact list of endpoints depends on the Managed version. The authoritative reference is the Cluster API explorer, available from the CMC, which documents every route and lets you try it.

Step-by-step tutorial

Step 1 — Create a dedicated Cluster API token

In the CMC, open Settings > API tokens, Cluster tokens section, and create one token per use: {% raw %}audit, environment-provisioning, and so on. Tick only the permissions you need among Service Provider API (ServiceProviderAPI, required for environments, users, groups and nodes), Cluster token management, Read settings and Write settings. Store the value in your secrets vault; it will not be shown again.

export DT_CLUSTER="https://{your-domain}"
export DT_CTOKEN="{token}"   # load from a vault, never hard-coded in a repository

Step 2 — First call: list environments 

curl -s -H "Authorization: Api-Token $DT_CTOKEN" \
  -H "Accept: application/json" \
  "$DT_CLUSTER/api/cluster/v2/environments" | python3 -m json.tool

You get the list of environments with their ID, name, state and quotas. A 401 means token authentication failed: check its validity and permissions.

Step 3 — Create an environment idempotently

A good automation script can be rerun without side effects. So we check whether the environment exists before creating it:

#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail
NOM="${1:?usage: $0 environment-name}"

existe=$(curl -s -H "Authorization: Api-Token $DT_CTOKEN" \
  "$DT_CLUSTER/api/cluster/v2/environments" \
  | python3 -c "import sys,json; d=json.load(sys.stdin); print(any(e.get('name')=='$NOM' for e in d.get('environments',[])))")

if [ "$existe" = "True" ]; then
  echo "Environment $NOM already exists, nothing to do."
  exit 0
fi

curl -s -X POST -H "Authorization: Api-Token $DT_CTOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d "{\"name\": \"$NOM\", \"state\": \"ENABLED\", \"tags\": [\"provisionne-par-api\"]}" \
  "$DT_CLUSTER/api/cluster/v2/environments"

The list comes back in the environments array and is paginated (nextPageKey): on a large cluster, follow the pagination or raise pageSize. The creation response contains the new environment’s ID, which you should keep for the next steps.

Step 4 — Bootstrap the environment with a token

By adding ?createToken=true to the creation POST, the response contains a tokenManagementToken (scopes apiTokens.read, apiTokens.write and TenantTokenManagement). It lets you create, through POST /e/{id}/api/v2/apiTokens, an environment token with limited scopes. That token drives a second phase of scripts that pushes the baseline configuration through the environment API: automatic tags, management zones, alerting profiles.

export DT_ENV="$DT_CLUSTER/e/{environment-id}"
curl -s -H "Authorization: Api-Token {environment-token}" \
  "$DT_ENV/api/v2/settings/schemas" | python3 -m json.tool | head -40

Step 5 — Check node status before maintenance

Query the v1 route that returns the cluster’s known nodes (Service Provider API permission), including their operationState and version, and refuse to continue if a node is not in the expected state:

curl -s -H "Authorization: Api-Token $DT_CTOKEN" \
  "$DT_CLUSTER/api/v1.0/onpremise/cluster" | python3 -m json.tool

Combined with a systemctl or a df -h /var/opt/dynatrace-managed run on each node through your configuration management tool, this check makes a reliable maintenance « pre-flight check ».

Step 6 — Integrate with existing tooling

The same calls fit easily into Ansible (the uri module), a CI pipeline, or Terraform through a provider compatible with your version. The principle stays the same: a Git repository describes the desired state (environments, groups, quotas), and a job compares it with the actual state and applies the difference.

Best practices

  • One token per use, minimal scopes, an expiry date, scheduled rotation.
  • Never a plain-text token in a script, a repository or shell history; use a vault and environment variables.
  • Idempotence: check before creating, update rather than recreate.
  • Dry-run mode: print the action plan before applying it.
  • Error handling: check the HTTP code (curl -w "%{http_code}") and respect rate limits (429 response).
  • Regression tests after every Managed update: APIs evolve, and v1 routes may be deprecated in favour of v2.
  • Traceability: every automated action must be visible in the audit log and linked to a commit.

Frequently asked questions

What is the difference between the Cluster API and the environment API?

The Cluster API (/api/cluster/v2 and /api/v1.0/onpremise, cluster token created in the CMC) covers the platform: nodes, environments, users, groups, licences. The environment API (/e/{id}/api/…, environment token) covers monitoring: entities, metrics, problems, settings. Full automation often chains the two.

What do 401, 403 and 429 errors mean?

A 401 means token authentication failed (invalid, expired or missing the required permission), a 403 that access is denied, and a 429 that you have hit the rate limits: slow your calls down and retry later.

Where can you find the exact list of available routes?

In the Cluster API explorer, available from the CMC: it documents every route for your version and lets you try it. Recheck your scripts after each update, as some v1 routes may be deprecated in favour of v2.

Conclusion

The Cluster API is the tool that takes Dynatrace Managed administration from hand-crafted clicking to industrial-grade operations. By starting with simple, idempotent scripts — inventory, environment creation, audit export — and then plugging them into your configuration tooling, you gain speed, consistency across clusters and traceability. All without ever leaving the standards: HTTP, JSON, curl and a vault for secrets.

title: CloudWatch Logs retention policy for the whole account
summary:
A CloudWatch Logs retention policy is one of those settings nobody thinks about on the first deployment. Every Lambda function writes logs, and CloudWatch keeps them forever by default. After a few years of Serverless you end up with hundreds of log groups, and half of them belong to functions that no longer exist.

Since November 9, 2026, you can fix that centrally. An account-level retention policy defines how long logs stay in all log groups or in a selected subset. That sounds like a checkbox in the console. However, there is one detail in it that can delete data without warning. In this article I show you how the rules work, how to roll them out safely with a dry run, and how to manage them as code with AWS CDK.

In short

CloudWatch Logs can now set retention through policies for the whole account or for prefixes such as /aws/lambda. When several policies match, the longest one wins. The catch: a policy also replaces longer settings on individual log groups, so every change deserves a dry run first.

What you will learn in this article

  • How account-level policies decide the retention of log groups
  • Why a 90-day baseline can delete some logs earlier than you expect
  • How to check the impact first with a dry run and a small TypeScript tool
  • How to manage the policy as code with AWS CDK

Why log retention gets forgotten so often

CloudWatch Logs stores log data indefinitely by default. The documentation says so, and in day-to-day work you hardly notice. A Lambda function creates its log group /aws/lambda/ on the first invocation if you did not define it in your infrastructure code. It then says “Never expire”, and nobody ever looks at it again.

In addition, these log groups stay behind when you delete a stack. The function is gone, the logs remain. That costs storage, and it is also a privacy topic: logs like to contain email addresses, IP addresses or order numbers. The GDPR includes the principle of storage limitation (Art. 5(1)(e)), and “forever” is rarely a good answer to it. This is not legal advice, but it is a good reason to stop postponing the topic.

Until now you had two options. Either every team sets retention per log group in code. Or a platform group builds a Lambda function that catches new log groups via EventBridge and sets a retention afterwards. Both work, both have gaps. That is exactly where the new feature comes in.

How a CloudWatch Logs retention policy works

An account-level retention policy is an entry per account and Region that you create through the PutAccountPolicy API with the type RETENTION_POLICY. It has four parts:

Part Meaning Allowed values
Name unique name in the account free text, must not start with aws/
Retention how long log events are kept 30, 60, 90, 120, 150, 180, 365, 400, 545, 731, 1096, 1827, 2192, 2557, 2922, 3288, 3653 days or NEVER_EXPIRE
Enforcement mode does the rule also apply to existing log groups? RETROACTIVE or NEW_ONLY
Selection which log groups no filter (all) or LogGroupNamePrefix="/aws/lambda"

You can create up to 20 of these policies per Region. The feature costs nothing extra, and according to the announcement it is available in all commercial Regions except Bahrain and the United Arab Emirates. Important: a policy only applies in the Region where you create it. If you work in eu-central-1 and eu-west-1, you need it twice.

The longest policy wins

Unlike other account-level policies in CloudWatch, retention policies may overlap. If several match a log group, the one with the longest retention applies. NEVER_EXPIRE counts as the longest. This leads to a nice pattern: one baseline for everything, longer periods for certain prefixes, and exceptions that never expire.

Example with three policies: the longest matching policy determines the effective retention.

The catch: longer settings get replaced too

Now comes the part you should not skim. A matching account-level policy fully replaces the setting of the log group. That works in both directions. If a log group keeps data for ten years and you create a 90-day baseline for everything, CloudWatch deletes everything in it that is older than 90 days. The documentation explicitly warns about this.

The opposite case is surprising as well. Many teams deliberately use 7 or 14 days for Lambda logs. Account-level policies, on the other hand, require at least 30 days. If such a log group falls under your baseline, it suddenly gets 30 or 90 days and costs more storage than before. So a baseline is a fixed value for everything it matches, and it is no upper limit.

RETROACTIVE or NEW_ONLY?

With RETROACTIVE, the policy applies to every matching log group, including existing ones. With NEW_ONLY, it only applies to log groups created after the policy. Existing ones keep their own setting. NEW_ONLY is the cautious start, yet it does not clean up the old leftovers. I would begin with a dry run for RETROACTIVE and decide after that.

Two timing details: a new or updated policy only takes effect after about 24 hours. Until then, the old value applies. Also, CloudWatch typically deletes expired events within 72 hours, in rare cases later. From the moment they expire, though, they no longer count towards storage costs.

🎬 How CloudWatch Logs determines the effective retention of a log group – this animated diagram only runs on my site: watch it on sascha-ms.de

Step by step: roll out retention with the AWS CLI

This is how I would introduce a CloudWatch Logs retention policy in an existing account. You need:

  • AWS CLI v2 in a recent version whose put-account-policy command knows the --dry-run parameter
  • the permissions logs:PutAccountPolicy and logs:PutRetentionPolicy, for deleting logs:DeleteAccountPolicy and logs:DeleteRetentionPolicy, for reading logs:DescribeAccountPolicies and logs:DescribeLogGroups
  • an idea of which logs must stay longer (audit, billing, contracts)

1. Take stock

First, check which log groups never expire today and how much they store:

aws logs describe-log-groups \
  --query 'logGroups[?!retentionInDays].[logGroupName, storedBytes]' \
  --output table

The result is a table with names and stored bytes. Write down the log groups that should deliberately live longer. Those are exactly the ones that need their own policy in a moment.

2. Create the exceptions first

Create the longer periods before the baseline. That way there is no moment in which only the short baseline applies. In this example, the fictional bike rental keeps its audit logs for two years:

aws logs put-account-policy \
  --policy-name audit-2y \
  --policy-type RETENTION_POLICY \
  --policy-document '{"retentionInDays": 731, "enforcementMode": "RETROACTIVE"}' \
  --selection-criteria 'LogGroupNamePrefix="/bikerental/audit"'

3. Check the baseline with a dry run

Next comes the baseline for everything. With --dry-run, CloudWatch saves nothing. Instead, it reports how many log groups would keep data longer, shorter or unchanged:

aws logs put-account-policy \
  --policy-name baseline-90d \
  --policy-type RETENTION_POLICY \
  --policy-document '{"retentionInDays": 90, "enforcementMode": "RETROACTIVE"}' \
  --dry-run

The response contains a dryRunResult object with the fields decreasedRetentionLogGroupCount, increasedRetentionLogGroupCount and unchangedRetentionLogGroupCount. It also lists up to 20 of the largest affected log groups. For example, you immediately see whether a large archive group would get shorter. If decreasedRetentionLogGroupCount is greater than zero, look closely: those are the log groups that lose data.

4. Create it and check after 24 hours

If everything looks right, send the same command without --dry-run. After about a day, describe-log-groups shows the effective retention and the name of the policy that decides it:

aws logs describe-log-groups \
  --log-group-name-prefix /aws/lambda \
  --query 'logGroups[].[logGroupName, retentionInDays, retentionPolicyName]' \
  --output table

The retentionPolicyName field only shows up when an account-level policy applies. If NEVER_EXPIRE applies, retentionInDays is missing from the response. To list all policies, run aws logs describe-account-policies --policy-type RETENTION_POLICY.

A TypeScript tool for plan and dry run

The dry run returns counts and the 20 largest log groups. Often that is enough. But if you want to see the complete list of groups that lose data before an approval, a small tool helps. It loads all log groups and existing policies, recalculates the rules locally and then also asks for the real dry run.

Its core is pure logic without AWS calls and therefore easy to test. The effectiveRetention function implements both rules from above: the longest matching policy wins, and it replaces the log group’s own value.

// src/retention.ts
// Pure planning logic for account-level CloudWatch Logs retention policies.
// No AWS calls in here, so everything can be unit-tested offline.

/** Retention values (in days) that account-level policies accept. */
export const ALLOWED_DAYS = [
  30, 60, 90, 120, 150, 180, 365, 400, 545, 731, 1096, 1827, 2192, 2557, 2922,
  3288, 3653,
] as const;

export type Retention = number | "NEVER_EXPIRE";
export type EnforcementMode = "RETROACTIVE" | "NEW_ONLY";

export interface RetentionPolicy {
  name: string;
  /** Log group name prefix; undefined = all log groups in the account. */
  prefix?: string;
  retention: Retention;
  mode: EnforcementMode;
  /** When the policy was created (epoch ms). Needed for NEW_ONLY. */
  createdAt: number;
}

export interface LogGroupInfo {
  name: string;
  /** Retention set on the log group itself; undefined = never expire. */
  retentionInDays?: number;
  creationTime: number;
  storedBytes: number;
}

export type ChangeKind = "shorter" | "longer" | "unchanged";

export interface PlannedChange {
  group: LogGroupInfo;
  before: Retention;
  after: Retention;
  kind: ChangeKind;
  /** Name of the policy that decides the retention after the change. */
  decidedBy?: string;
}

/** Parses CLI input like "90" or "never" into a valid retention value. */
export function parseRetention(input: string): Retention {
  const value = input.trim().toLowerCase();
  if (value === "never" || value === "never_expire") return "NEVER_EXPIRE";
  const days = Number(value);
  if (!Number.isInteger(days) || !(ALLOWED_DAYS as readonly number[]).includes(days)) {
    throw new Error(
      `Invalid retention "${input}". Allowed: ${ALLOWED_DAYS.join(", ")} or "never".`,
    );
  }
  return days;
}

/** Builds the policyDocument string for PutAccountPolicy. */
export function buildPolicyDocument(retention: Retention, mode: EnforcementMode): string {
  return JSON.stringify({ retentionInDays: retention, enforcementMode: mode });
}

/** Builds the selectionCriteria string, or undefined for "all log groups". */
export function buildSelectionCriteria(prefix?: string): string | undefined {
  if (prefix === undefined || prefix === "") return undefined;
  if (prefix.includes('"')) throw new Error("Prefix must not contain double quotes.");
  return `LogGroupNamePrefix="${prefix}"`;
}

/** Reads a policy as returned by DescribeAccountPolicies. */
export function parsePolicy(p: {
  policyName?: string;
  policyDocument?: string;
  selectionCriteria?: string;
  lastUpdatedTime?: number;
}): RetentionPolicy {
  const doc = JSON.parse(p.policyDocument ?? "{}") as {
    retentionInDays?: Retention;
    enforcementMode?: EnforcementMode;
  };
  const match = /LogGroupNamePrefix\s*=\s*"([^"]*)"/.exec(p.selectionCriteria ?? "");
  return {
    name: p.policyName ?? "unknown",
    prefix: match?.[1],
    retention: doc.retentionInDays ?? "NEVER_EXPIRE",
    mode: doc.enforcementMode ?? "RETROACTIVE",
    // The API only returns lastUpdatedTime, which is the best approximation we have.
    createdAt: p.lastUpdatedTime ?? 0,
  };
}

/** Does a policy apply to a given log group? */
export function policyMatches(policy: RetentionPolicy, group: LogGroupInfo): boolean {
  const prefixOk = policy.prefix === undefined || group.name.startsWith(policy.prefix);
  const modeOk = policy.mode === "RETROACTIVE" || group.creationTime >= policy.createdAt;
  return prefixOk && modeOk;
}

/** Compares two retention values. NEVER_EXPIRE is the longest. */
export function compareRetention(a: Retention, b: Retention): number {
  const toNumber = (r: Retention) => (r === "NEVER_EXPIRE" ? Number.POSITIVE_INFINITY : r);
  return toNumber(a) - toNumber(b);
}

/**
 * Effective retention of a log group: if at least one account policy matches,
 * the longest matching policy wins and REPLACES the log group's own setting
 * (even if that setting was longer). Otherwise the log group's own value counts.
 */
export function effectiveRetention(
  group: LogGroupInfo,
  policies: RetentionPolicy[],
): { retention: Retention; decidedBy?: string } {
  const matching = policies.filter((p) => policyMatches(p, group));
  if (matching.length === 0) {
    return { retention: group.retentionInDays ?? "NEVER_EXPIRE" };
  }
  const winner = matching.reduce((best, p) =>
    compareRetention(p.retention, best.retention) > 0 ? p : best,
  );
  return { retention: winner.retention, decidedBy: winner.name };
}

/** Simulates adding (or replacing) a policy and lists the effect per log group. */
export function planChange(
  groups: LogGroupInfo[],
  existing: RetentionPolicy[],
  candidate: RetentionPolicy,
): PlannedChange[] {
  const after = [...existing.filter((p) => p.name !== candidate.name), candidate];
  return groups
    .map((group) => {
      const before = effectiveRetention(group, existing).retention;
      const next = effectiveRetention(group, after);
      const diff = compareRetention(next.retention, before);
      const kind: ChangeKind = diff < 0 ? "shorter" : diff > 0 ? "longer" : "unchanged";
      return { group, before, after: next.retention, kind, decidedBy: next.decidedBy };
    })
    .sort((a, b) => b.group.storedBytes - a.group.storedBytes);
}

/** Groups the plan by kind, e.g. for a short summary. */

// lib/log-retention-stack.ts
// CloudFormation's AWS::Logs::AccountPolicy does not list RETENTION_POLICY yet,
// so this stack calls the CloudWatch Logs API through an AwsCustomResource.
import { Stack, type StackProps } from "aws-cdk-lib";
import * as iam from "aws-cdk-lib/aws-iam";
import {
  AwsCustomResource,
  AwsCustomResourcePolicy,
  PhysicalResourceId,
} from "aws-cdk-lib/custom-resources";
import { Construct } from "constructs";

export interface RetentionRule {
  /** Unique policy name, must not start with "aws/". */
  name: string;
  /** Log group name prefix; leave empty for all log groups. */
  prefix?: string;
  /** 30, 60, 90, ... 3653 or "NEVER_EXPIRE". */
  retention: number | "NEVER_EXPIRE";
  mode?: "RETROACTIVE" | "NEW_ONLY";
}

export class AccountRetentionPolicy extends Construct {
  constructor(scope: Construct, id: string, rule: RetentionRule) {
    super(scope, id);

    const params: Record<string, string> = {
      policyName: rule.name,
      policyType: "RETENTION_POLICY",
      policyDocument: JSON.stringify({
        retentionInDays: rule.retention,
        enforcementMode: rule.mode ?? "RETROACTIVE",
      }),
    };
    if (rule.prefix) {
      params.selectionCriteria = `LogGroupNamePrefix="${rule.prefix}"`;
    }

    const putCall = {
      service: "CloudWatchLogs",
      action: "putAccountPolicy",

      onUpdate: putCall,

        action: "deleteAccountPolicy",

      },
      policy: AwsCustomResourcePolicy.fromStatements([
        new iam.PolicyStatement({
          actions: [
            "logs:PutAccountPolicy",
            "logs:PutRetentionPolicy",
            "logs:DeleteAccountPolicy",
            "logs:DeleteRetentionPolicy",

    });

export class LogRetentionStack extends Stack {
  constructor(scope: Construct, id: string, props?: StackProps) {
    super(scope, id, props);

    // Baseline for everything in this account and region.
    new AccountRetentionPolicy(this, "Baseline", { name: "baseline-90d", retention: 90 });

    // Longer retention for audit logs of the fictional bike rental.
    new AccountRetentionPolicy(this, "Audit", {

If you delete the stack, the policies disappear as well. A dry run of delete-account-policy shows you beforehand what will then apply to each log group.

A tip from the architecture corner: once prefixes decide about retention, log group names suddenly become an architecture decision. Write the convention down, for example in an architecture decision record. Otherwise an audit log will eventually end up under a prefix that cleans up after 90 days.

Common mistakes with log retention

  • Creating the baseline before the exceptions. The exceptions go in first, otherwise only the short period applies for a moment. The 24-hour delay softens that a bit, but I would not rely on it.
  • Skipping the dry run. A look at decreasedRetentionLogGroupCount takes seconds. Deleted logs do not come back.
  • Trusting the value in your code. If your team sets 14 days in a CDK stack, but an account-level policy applies, the policy value wins. Every team should know that.
  • Forgetting Regions. Each Region needs its own policies, including the one where only “a little bit” runs.
  • Granting too many permissions. AWS recommends giving logs:PutAccountPolicy only to administrators who own logging for the whole account.
  • Starting several dry runs at once. Only one dry run can run per account at a time. Scripts that check in parallel will get errors.

Keeping an eye on cost and security

The policies themselves are free. What changes is the storage cost of log data, and it can move in both directions. Old log groups without expiry get cheaper, while short Lambda log groups below 30 days may get more expensive. How much that means for you follows from the inventory in step 1 together with the CloudWatch Logs price list.

Security is mostly about control. Whoever may change account-level policies can indirectly delete logs. Treat these permissions like delete permissions. For logs with a legal retention requirement, I would also check whether they belong in a central log archive account to which application teams have no write access.

My take

To be honest: I have been waiting for this for a long time. “Never expire” as the default was always a poor compromise for Serverless accounts with many small functions. Finally there is a built-in solution, without a custom cleanup Lambda.

Still, I would like different semantics. A baseline that replaces longer values on individual log groups is handy for platform teams and surprising for application teams. An option like “only set it if nothing is set” would save a lot of discussions. Until then, communication is the only fix: tell the teams that their value in code no longer has the last word. And put it into your runbook before someone searches for logs during an incident that no longer exist.

My suggestion for the start: a 90-day baseline with RETROACTIVE, exceptions for audit and contracts created first, everything checked with a dry run and managed as code. That takes an hour and cleans up years of leftovers.

FAQ

How long does CloudWatch Logs keep logs by default?

Indefinitely. Without its own setting and without an account-level policy, log events never expire.

Can I set a 7-day retention with an account-level policy?

No. Account-level policies require at least 30 days. Shorter periods still only work per log group, and only as long as no account-level policy applies to that group.

Does the retention policy cost extra?

No, according to AWS there are no additional costs for the policies. Only the storage costs of the log data change.

How do I delete a retention policy again?

Use aws logs delete-account-policy --policy-name --policy-type RETENTION_POLICY. Add --dry-run to see the effect of the deletion first.

Your next step

Run the inventory from step 1 in your most important account today. The number of log groups set to “Never expire” is usually argument enough. If you are working on costs anyway, my article about NAT gateway costs with Lambda fits right in.

Now it is your turn: which baseline retention do you consider sensible, and which logs have to stay longer in your setup? Let me know in the comments.

event_model_payload.summary:
A CloudWatch Logs retention policy is one of those settings nobody thinks about on the first deployment. Every Lambda function writes logs, and CloudWatch keeps them forever by default. After a few years of Serverless you end up with hundreds of log groups, and half of them belong to functions that no longer exist.

Since November 9, 2026, you can fix that centrally. An account-level retention policy defines how long logs stay in all log groups or in a selected subset. That sounds like a checkbox in the console. However, there is one detail in it that can delete data without warning. In this article I show you how the rules work, how to roll them out safely with a dry run, and how to manage them as code with AWS CDK.

In short

CloudWatch Logs can now set retention through policies for the whole account or for prefixes such as /aws/lambda. When several policies match, the longest one wins. The catch: a policy also replaces longer settings on individual log groups, so every change deserves a dry run first.

What you will learn in this article

  • How account-level policies decide the retention of log groups
  • Why a 90-day baseline can delete some logs earlier than you expect
  • How to check the impact first with a dry run and a small TypeScript tool
  • How to manage the policy as code with AWS CDK

Why log retention gets forgotten so often

CloudWatch Logs stores log data indefinitely by default. The documentation says so, and in day-to-day work you hardly notice. A Lambda function creates its log group /aws/lambda/ on the first invocation if you did not define it in your infrastructure code. It then says “Never expire”, and nobody ever looks at it again.

In addition, these log groups stay behind when you delete a stack. The function is gone, the logs remain. That costs storage, and it is also a privacy topic: logs like to contain email addresses, IP addresses or order numbers. The GDPR includes the principle of storage limitation (Art. 5(1)(e)), and “forever” is rarely a good answer to it. This is not legal advice, but it is a good reason to stop postponing the topic.

Until now you had two options. Either every team sets retention per log group in code. Or a platform group builds a Lambda function that catches new log groups via EventBridge and sets a retention afterwards. Both work, both have gaps. That is exactly where the new feature comes in.

How a CloudWatch Logs retention policy works

An account-level retention policy is an entry per account and Region that you create through the PutAccountPolicy API with the type RETENTION_POLICY. It has four parts:

Part Meaning Allowed values
Name unique name in the account free text, must not start with aws/
Retention how long log events are kept 30, 60, 90, 120, 150, 180, 365, 400, 545, 731, 1096, 1827, 2192, 2557, 2922, 3288, 3653 days or NEVER_EXPIRE
Enforcement mode does the rule also apply to existing log groups? RETROACTIVE or NEW_ONLY
Selection which log groups no filter (all) or LogGroupNamePrefix="/aws/lambda"

You can create up to 20 of these policies per Region. The feature costs nothing extra, and according to the announcement it is available in all commercial Regions except Bahrain and the United Arab Emirates. Important: a policy only applies in the Region where you create it. If you work in eu-central-1 and eu-west-1, you need it twice.

The longest policy wins

Unlike other account-level policies in CloudWatch, retention policies may overlap. If several match a log group, the one with the longest retention applies. NEVER_EXPIRE counts as the longest. This leads to a nice pattern: one baseline for everything, longer periods for certain prefixes, and exceptions that never expire.

Example with three policies: the longest matching policy determines the effective retention.

The catch: longer settings get replaced too

Now comes the part you should not skim. A matching account-level policy fully replaces the setting of the log group. That works in both directions. If a log group keeps data for ten years and you create a 90-day baseline for everything, CloudWatch deletes everything in it that is older than 90 days. The documentation explicitly warns about this.

The opposite case is surprising as well. Many teams deliberately use 7 or 14 days for Lambda logs. Account-level policies, on the other hand, require at least 30 days. If such a log group falls under your baseline, it suddenly gets 30 or 90 days and costs more storage than before. So a baseline is a fixed value for everything it matches, and it is no upper limit.

RETROACTIVE or NEW_ONLY?

With RETROACTIVE, the policy applies to every matching log group, including existing ones. With NEW_ONLY, it only applies to log groups created after the policy. Existing ones keep their own setting. NEW_ONLY is the cautious start, yet it does not clean up the old leftovers. I would begin with a dry run for RETROACTIVE and decide after that.

Two timing details: a new or updated policy only takes effect after about 24 hours. Until then, the old value applies. Also, CloudWatch typically deletes expired events within 72 hours, in rare cases later. From the moment they expire, though, they no longer count towards storage costs.

🎬 How CloudWatch Logs determines the effective retention of a log group – this animated diagram only runs on my site: watch it on sascha-ms.de

Step by step: roll out retention with the AWS CLI

This is how I would introduce a CloudWatch Logs retention policy in an existing account. You need:

  • AWS CLI v2 in a recent version whose put-account-policy command knows the --dry-run parameter
  • the permissions logs:PutAccountPolicy and logs:PutRetentionPolicy, for deleting logs:DeleteAccountPolicy and logs:DeleteRetentionPolicy, for reading logs:DescribeAccountPolicies and logs:DescribeLogGroups
  • an idea of which logs must stay longer (audit, billing, contracts)

1. Take stock

First, check which log groups never expire today and how much they store:

aws logs describe-log-groups \
  --query 'logGroups[?!retentionInDays].[logGroupName, storedBytes]' \
  --output table

The result is a table with names and stored bytes. Write down the log groups that should deliberately live longer. Those are exactly the ones that need their own policy in a moment.

2. Create the exceptions first

Create the longer periods before the baseline. That way there is no moment in which only the short baseline applies. In this example, the fictional bike rental keeps its audit logs for two years:

aws logs put-account-policy \
  --policy-name audit-2y \
  --policy-type RETENTION_POLICY \
  --policy-document '{"retentionInDays": 731, "enforcementMode": "RETROACTIVE"}' \
  --selection-criteria 'LogGroupNamePrefix="/bikerental/audit"'

3. Check the baseline with a dry run

Next comes the baseline for everything. With --dry-run, CloudWatch saves nothing. Instead, it reports how many log groups would keep data longer, shorter or unchanged:

aws logs put-account-policy \
  --policy-name baseline-90d \
  --policy-type RETENTION_POLICY \
  --policy-document '{"retentionInDays": 90, "enforcementMode": "RETROACTIVE"}' \
  --dry-run

The response contains a dryRunResult object with the fields decreasedRetentionLogGroupCount, increasedRetentionLogGroupCount and unchangedRetentionLogGroupCount. It also lists up to 20 of the largest affected log groups. For example, you immediately see whether a large archive group would get shorter. If decreasedRetentionLogGroupCount is greater than zero, look closely: those are the log groups that lose data.

4. Create it and check after 24 hours

If everything looks right, send the same command without --dry-run. After about a day, describe-log-groups shows the effective retention and the name of the policy that decides it:

aws logs describe-log-groups \
  --log-group-name-prefix /aws/lambda \
  --query 'logGroups[].[logGroupName, retentionInDays, retentionPolicyName]' \
  --output table

The retentionPolicyName field only shows up when an account-level policy applies. If NEVER_EXPIRE applies, retentionInDays is missing from the response. To list all policies, run aws logs describe-account-policies --policy-type RETENTION_POLICY.

A TypeScript tool for plan and dry run

The dry run returns counts and the 20 largest log groups. Often that is enough. But if you want to see the complete list of groups that lose data before an approval, a small tool helps. It loads all log groups and existing policies, recalculates the rules locally and then also asks for the real dry run.

Its core is pure logic without AWS calls and therefore easy to test. The effectiveRetention function implements both rules from above: the longest matching policy wins, and it replaces the log group’s own value.

// src/retention.ts
// Pure planning logic for account-level CloudWatch Logs retention policies.
// No AWS calls in here, so everything can be unit-tested offline.

/** Retention values (in days) that account-level policies accept. */
export const ALLOWED_DAYS = [
  30, 60, 90, 120, 150, 180, 365, 400, 545, 731, 1096, 1827, 2192, 2557, 2922,
  3288, 3653,
] as const;

export type Retention = number | "NEVER_EXPIRE";
export type EnforcementMode = "RETROACTIVE" | "NEW_ONLY";

export interface RetentionPolicy {
  name: string;
  /** Log group name prefix; undefined = all log groups in the account. */
  prefix?: string;
  retention: Retention;
  mode: EnforcementMode;
  /** When the policy was created (epoch ms). Needed for NEW_ONLY. */
  createdAt: number;
}

export interface LogGroupInfo {
  name: string;
  /** Retention set on the log group itself; undefined = never expire. */
  retentionInDays?: number;
  creationTime: number;
  storedBytes: number;
}

export type ChangeKind = "shorter" | "longer" | "unchanged";

export interface PlannedChange {
  group: LogGroupInfo;
  before: Retention;
  after: Retention;
  kind: ChangeKind;
  /** Name of the policy that decides the retention after the change. */
  decidedBy?: string;
}

/** Parses CLI input like "90" or "never" into a valid retention value. */
export function parseRetention(input: string): Retention {
  const value = input.trim().toLowerCase();
  if (value === "never" || value === "never_expire") return "NEVER_EXPIRE";
  const days = Number(value);
  if (!Number.isInteger(days) || !(ALLOWED_DAYS as readonly number[]).includes(days)) {
    throw new Error(
      `Invalid retention "${input}". Allowed: ${ALLOWED_DAYS.join(", ")} or "never".`,
    );
  }
  return days;
}

/** Builds the policyDocument string for PutAccountPolicy. */
export function buildPolicyDocument(retention: Retention, mode: EnforcementMode): string {
  return JSON.stringify({ retentionInDays: retention, enforcementMode: mode });
}

/** Builds the selectionCriteria string, or undefined for "all log groups". */
export function buildSelectionCriteria(prefix?: string): string | undefined {
  if (prefix === undefined || prefix === "") return undefined;
  if (prefix.includes('"')) throw new Error("Prefix must not contain double quotes.");
  return `LogGroupNamePrefix="${prefix}"`;
}

/** Reads a policy as returned by DescribeAccountPolicies. */
export function parsePolicy(p: {
  policyName?: string;
  policyDocument?: string;
  selectionCriteria?: string;
  lastUpdatedTime?: number;
}): RetentionPolicy {
  const doc = JSON.parse(p.policyDocument ?? "{}") as {
    retentionInDays?: Retention;
    enforcementMode?: EnforcementMode;
  };
  const match = /LogGroupNamePrefix\s*=\s*"([^"]*)"/.exec(p.selectionCriteria ?? "");
  return {
    name: p.policyName ?? "unknown",
    prefix: match?.[1],
    retention: doc.retentionInDays ?? "NEVER_EXPIRE",
    mode: doc.enforcementMode ?? "RETROACTIVE",
    // The API only returns lastUpdatedTime, which is the best approximation we have.
    createdAt: p.lastUpdatedTime ?? 0,
  };
}

/** Does a policy apply to a given log group? */
export function policyMatches(policy: RetentionPolicy, group: LogGroupInfo): boolean {
  const prefixOk = policy.prefix === undefined || group.name.startsWith(policy.prefix);
  const modeOk = policy.mode === "RETROACTIVE" || group.creationTime >= policy.createdAt;
  return prefixOk && modeOk;
}

/** Compares two retention values. NEVER_EXPIRE is the longest. */
export function compareRetention(a: Retention, b: Retention): number {
  const toNumber = (r: Retention) => (r === "NEVER_EXPIRE" ? Number.POSITIVE_INFINITY : r);
  return toNumber(a) - toNumber(b);
}

/**
 * Effective retention of a log group: if at least one account policy matches,
 * the longest matching policy wins and REPLACES the log group's own setting
 * (even if that setting was longer). Otherwise the log group's own value counts.
 */
export function effectiveRetention(
  group: LogGroupInfo,
  policies: RetentionPolicy[],
): { retention: Retention; decidedBy?: string } {
  const matching = policies.filter((p) => policyMatches(p, group));
  if (matching.length === 0) {
    return { retention: group.retentionInDays ?? "NEVER_EXPIRE" };
  }
  const winner = matching.reduce((best, p) =>
    compareRetention(p.retention, best.retention) > 0 ? p : best,
  );
  return { retention: winner.retention, decidedBy: winner.name };
}

/** Simulates adding (or replacing) a policy and lists the effect per log group. */
export function planChange(
  groups: LogGroupInfo[],
  existing: RetentionPolicy[],
  candidate: RetentionPolicy,
): PlannedChange[] {
  const after = [...existing.filter((p) => p.name !== candidate.name), candidate];
  return groups
    .map((group) => {
      const before = effectiveRetention(group, existing).retention;
      const next = effectiveRetention(group, after);
      const diff = compareRetention(next.retention, before);
      const kind: ChangeKind = diff < 0 ? "shorter" : diff > 0 ? "longer" : "unchanged";
      return { group, before, after: next.retention, kind, decidedBy: next.decidedBy };
    })
    .sort((a, b) => b.group.storedBytes - a.group.storedBytes);
}

  const summary: Record = { shorter: 0, longer: 0, unchanged: 0 };
  for (const change of plan) summary[change.kind] += 1;
  return summary;
}

  const units = ["B", "KiB", "MiB", "GiB", "TiB"];
  let value = bytes;

  }
  return `${value.toFixed(unit === 0 ? 0 : 1)} ${units[unit]}`;

A tip from the architecture corner: once prefixes decide about retention, log group names suddenly become an architecture decision. Write the convention down, for example in an architecture decision record. Otherwise an audit log will eventually end up under a prefix that cleans up after 90 days.

Common mistakes with log retention

  • Creating the baseline before the exceptions. The exceptions go in first, otherwise only the short period applies for a moment. The 24-hour delay softens that a bit, but I would not rely on it.
  • Skipping the dry run. A look at decreasedRetentionLogGroupCount takes seconds. Deleted logs do not come back.
  • Trusting the value in your code. If your team sets 14 days in a CDK stack, but an account-level policy applies, the policy value wins. Every team should know that.
  • Forgetting Regions. Each Region needs its own policies, including the one where only “a little bit” runs.
  • Granting too many permissions. AWS recommends giving logs:PutAccountPolicy only to administrators who own logging for the whole account.
  • Starting several dry runs at once. Only one dry run can run per account at a time. Scripts that check in parallel will get errors.

Keeping an eye on cost and security

The policies themselves are free. What changes is the storage cost of log data, and it can move in both directions. Old log groups without expiry get cheaper, while short Lambda log groups below 30 days may get more expensive. How much that means for you follows from the inventory in step 1 together with the CloudWatch Logs price list.

Security is mostly about control. Whoever may change account-level policies can indirectly delete logs. Treat these permissions like delete permissions. For logs with a legal retention requirement, I would also check whether they belong in a central log archive account to which application teams have no write access.

My take

To be honest: I have been waiting for this for a long time. “Never expire” as the default was always a poor compromise for Serverless accounts with many small functions. Finally there is a built-in solution, without a custom cleanup Lambda.

Still, I would like different semantics. A baseline that replaces longer values on individual log groups is handy for platform teams and surprising for application teams. An option like “only set it if nothing is set” would save a lot of discussions. Until then, communication is the only fix: tell the teams that their value in code no longer has the last word. And put it into your runbook before someone searches for logs during an incident that no longer exist.

My suggestion for the start: a 90-day baseline with RETROACTIVE, exceptions for audit and contracts created first, everything checked with a dry run and managed as code. That takes an hour and cleans up years of leftovers.

FAQ

Indefinitely. Without its own setting and without an account-level policy, log events never expire.

Can I set a 7-day retention with an account-level policy?

No. Account-level policies require at least 30 days. Shorter periods still only work per log group, and only as long as no account-level policy applies to that group.

Does the retention policy cost extra?

No, according to AWS there are no additional costs for the policies. Only the storage costs of the log data change.

Use aws logs delete-account-policy --policy-name --policy-type RETENTION_POLICY. Add --dry-run to see the effect of the deletion first.

Your next step

Run the inventory from step 1 in your most important account today. The number of log groups set to “Never expire” is usually argument enough. If you are working on costs anyway, my article about NAT gateway costs with Lambda fits right in.

Now it is your turn: which baseline retention do you consider sensible, and which logs have to stay longer in your setup? Let me know in the comments.

title: Azure API Management CI/CD: APIOps Pipelines with GitHub Actions
summary:
What has to pass before a merged pull request may change the production API Management instance without anyone opening the portal? Part 5's publish workflow already ran a dry run on every pull request and published on merge, but nothing required the dry run to pass, it signed in with the same identity that published to dev, and nothing read the spec or the policies before the CLI did. A pipeline you can trust with prod needs four gates, each catching something the others can't: checks that need no Azure at all, a dry run that can only read, a publish to dev that API Management itself validates, and a person who approves prod.

The companion repo keeps Part 5's layout: apiops/ holds the artifact tree, the extract filter and configuration.prod.yaml, and the APIOps CLI is still pinned at @azure-tools/apiops-cli@1.0.5. The publish workflow is what changes. The dry run becomes a required check that runs on every pull request and can only read, dev gets the merged commit, prod gets it after an approval, and a manual run publishes the full tree when prod has fallen behind. Each stage signs in through OIDC with its own user-assigned managed identity, so the repository holds no Azure secret. As in Part 5, nothing is deployed. Both workflows pass actionlint, the three validate steps ran locally against the sample, the claim that the dry run only reads comes from the CLI's 1.0.5 source, and no workflow has run on GitHub or exchanged a token with Entra ID. Where a step depends on how GitHub or Azure behaves at run time, I link the documentation it rests on.

From a local change to production

A change starts on a branch that edits something under ApimOrdersDemo/apiops/. Its pull request gets two checks. validate lints the specs, checks the policy files and compares each spec with the base branch, without signing in to Azure. dry-run signs in as id-apiops-plan, which can only read, and plans the change against dev, then against prod with the prod overrides. Both are required, so a merge waits for them. The merge lands one commit on main. publish-dev publishes that commit to dev as id-apiops-dev, then publish-prod waits in the prod environment until a reviewer approves and publishes the same commit to prod as id-apiops-prod. The nightly extract from Part 5 keeps running on the side and turns portal edits into drift pull requests, which pass through the same two checks as every other change.

The workflow is about 200 lines, most of them checkout, Node setup and CLI flags. Here is its job graph, with steps, runners, permissions and concurrency left out:

jobs:
  changes:
    if: github.event_name == 'pull_request'

  validate:      # required check, no Azure sign-in
    needs: changes
    if: needs.changes.outputs.validate == 'true'

  dry-run:       # required check, id-apiops-plan (Reader), no environment
    needs: changes
    if: needs.changes.outputs.apiops == 'true'

  publish-dev:   # id-apiops-dev

    needs: publish-dev
    environment: prod

On a pull request, the run takes changes and then validate and dry-run side by side. On a push to main or a manual run, it takes publish-dev and then publish-prod. Every job has an if: or a needs: that ties it to one of the two paths, so no run does both. The sections below show the parts of each job that matter.

Triggers: pull requests, pushes to main, and a manual full publish 

on:

  pull_request:

    paths: ['ApimOrdersDemo/apiops/**']
  # Full publish without --commit-id, to reconcile prod after a rejected or cancelled run.
  workflow_dispatch:

pull_request has no paths filter, on purpose. GitHub's workflow syntax reference spells out what a path filter does to a required check: when a workflow is skipped by path filtering, its checks "will remain in a 'Pending' state", and a pull request that requires them "will be blocked from merging." The samples repo has two dozen folders next to ApimOrdersDemo. So the workflow starts on every pull request and decides inside. A skipped job reports Success, even when it is a required check, which makes a job-level if: the answer: green for pull requests that don't touch apiops/, a real dry run for those that do. The changes job computes it:

  changes:
    if: github.event_name == 'pull_request'
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    outputs:
      apiops: ${{ steps.diff.outputs.apiops }}
      validate: ${{ steps.diff.outputs.validate }}
    steps:
      # A change to the policy script alone runs validate against the unchanged artifacts. It plans
      # nothing, so dry-run stays skipped.
      - id: diff
        run: |
          changed() { if git diff --quiet HEAD~1 HEAD -- "$@"; then echo false; else echo true; fi; }
          echo "apiops=$(changed ApimOrdersDemo/apiops)" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"
          echo "validate=$(changed ApimOrdersDemo/apiops ApimOrdersDemo/scripts/check-policies.mjs)" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"

On a pull request, actions/checkout checks out the merge commit GitHub builds for it, and that commit's first parent is the tip of the base branch. HEAD~1..HEAD is everything the pull request changes. It's also the range --commit-id diffs in the dry run (Part 5: ~1 against ), so the two can't disagree about whether apiops/ changed, and a checkout with fetch-depth: 2 is all the history either needs. There are two outputs because the two checks read different files. dry-run plans the artifacts, so apiops/ is all it cares about. validate also runs scripts/check-policies.mjs, which lives outside apiops/, and with one output a pull request that changed only the script would merge without the new script running once. workflow_dispatch takes no inputs. A manual run follows the same publish-dev and publish-prod path as a push, with one difference in the publish command:

          ${{ github.event_name == 'push' && format('--commit-id {0}', github.sha) || '' }}

On a push, the expression becomes --commit-id . On a manual run it's empty, and the CLI publishes the full tree. That's the reconcile path. Linting the OpenAPI specs 

      - name: Lint the OpenAPI specs

  59:9    error  operation-operationId  Operation must have "operationId".                             paths./orders/{orderId}.get

apis/orders/policy.xml:27: parser error : attributes construct error

The script never runs the C# in the expressions; it only finds where each one starts and ends.

      - name: Check the policies
        run: node ../scripts/check-policies.mjs apim-artifacts

It blanks every policy expression and parses what's left as XML. It then requires one inbound, backend, outbound and on-error section in every API, operation and product policy, each with a directly inside, and compares apis/orders/policy.xml with apis/orders-v2/policy.xml byte for byte. The blanking is what makes the parse possible:

// Expressions are C#, and policies travel as rawxml, so condition="@(x == "POST")" is a valid policy
// and invalid XML. Replace each @(...) and @{...} with spaces, keeping line breaks for line numbers.
function blankExpressions(src) {
  let out = ''
  for (let i = 0; i < src.length; i++) {
    const close = src[i] === '@' && { '(': ')', '{': '}' }[src[i + 1]]
    if (!close) {
      out += src[i]
      continue
    }
    let depth = 0
    let end = -1
    for (let j = i + 1; j < src.length && end < 0; j++) {
      if (src[j] === '"' || src[j] === "'") j = skipLiteral(src, j)
      else if (src[j] === src[i + 1]) depth++
      else if (src[j] === close && --depth === 0) end = j
    }
    if (end < 0) throw new PolicyError(src, i, 'unclosed policy expression')
    out += src.slice(i, end + 1).replace(/[^\n]/g, ' ')
    i = end
  }
  return out
}

The scan counts brackets and skips C# string and char literals, so a ) inside "..." doesn't end the expression. Spaces instead of an empty string keep every tag on its original line, which is the line the error message reports.

On the sample's six policy files it prints 6 policy files OK. On a copy with three typical mistakes, it exits 1: the get-order operation policy without in inbound, an unquoted attribute in the partner product's policy, and Part 5's Orders.Read role added to v1 only:

apis/orders/operations/get-order/policy.xml:  has no , so the broader scope's inbound section never runs
products/orders-partners/policy.xml: line 4: malformed markup (unquoted attribute, or < in an attribute value?)
apis/orders/policy.xml: differs from apis/orders-v2/policy.xml; change both

The rule is the reason the script exists. An operation policy without it skips the product rate limit, the token check and the backend route, and nothing reports an error. In this sample the call reaches the function without the managed identity token or the function key and gets a 401 from the backend instead of the gateway. The comparison is the sample-specific part: replace the pair in MUST_MATCH with yours, or delete it.

What the script can't know is which policy elements exist. parses and passes, and so does a {{named-value}} nobody created. Without a schema, only API Management can reject those, and its first chance is the PUT in publish-dev.

Copy the v2 spec over the v1 spec, commit, and the third step fails:

1 changes: 1 error, 0 warning, 0 info
error   [response-body-type-changed] at /head/apim-artifacts/apis/orders/specification.yaml
    in API GET /orders
        the response's body `type` changed from `array

title: Freestyle Job vs Declarative Pipeline in Jenkins: Which One Should You Use?
summary:
A beginner-friendly comparison of Jenkins Freestyle jobs and Declarative Pipelines on AWS EC2, with examples and a clear recommendation."
tags: aws, jenkins, devops, cicd

When I started learning Jenkins on AWS, the first question I hit was: "Should I create a Freestyle job or a Pipeline?" Both can build and deploy your code, but they work very differently. In this article I explain both in simple terms, compare them, and help you decide which one to use on your EC2-hosted Jenkins server.

What is a Freestyle Job?

A Freestyle job is the classic, beginner-friendly way to create a build in Jenkins. You configure everything through the web UI by clicking and filling in forms:

  • Choose a source code repository (GitHub)
  • Add a build trigger (manual, webhook, or poll SCM)
  • Add build steps (for example, "Execute shell")
  • Add post-build actions (for example, notifications)

Example: Docker build in a Freestyle job (Execute shell step)

docker build -t myuser/cloudcart:latest .
docker login -u $DOCKER_USER -p $DOCKER_PASS
docker push myuser/cloudcart:latest
docker run -d -p 8081:80 myuser/cloudcart:latest

Pros

  • Very easy to learn, with no coding needed
  • Fast to set up for simple tasks
  • Good for first labs and quick tests

Cons

  • The configuration lives inside Jenkins, not in your Git repository
  • Hard to copy, review, or version-control
  • Complex flows (multiple stages, parallel steps) get messy
  • If the Jenkins server is lost, the job setup is lost too

What is a Declarative Pipeline?

A Declarative Pipeline defines your whole CI/CD flow as code, in a file called a Jenkinsfile stored in your GitHub repo. It follows a clear, structured syntax made of stages and steps.

Example: Jenkinsfile

pipeline {
    agent any

    environment {
        IMAGE_NAME = "myuser/cloudcart"
    }

    stages {
        stage('Checkout') {
            steps {
                git branch: 'main', url: 'https://github.com/myuser/cloudcart.git'
            }
        }

        stage('Build Docker Image') {
            steps {
                sh 'docker build -t $IMAGE_NAME:latest .'
            }
        }

        stage('Push to Docker Hub') {
            steps {
                withCredentials([usernamePassword(credentialsId: 'dockerhub-creds',
                    usernameVariable: 'DOCKER_USER', passwordVariable: 'DOCKER_PASS')]) {
                    sh 'echo $DOCKER_PASS | docker login -u $DOCKER_USER --password-stdin'
                    sh 'docker push $IMAGE_NAME:latest'
                }
            }
        }

        stage('Deploy') {
            steps {
                sh 'docker rm -f cloudcart || true'
                sh 'docker run -d --name cloudcart -p 8081:80 $IMAGE_NAME:latest'
            }
        }
    }

    post {
        success { echo 'Pipeline completed successfully!' }
        failure { echo 'Pipeline failed. Check the logs.' }
    }
}

Pros

  • Pipeline as Code: it is versioned in Git with your application
  • A visual Stage View shows exactly which stage passed or failed
  • Easy to review, reuse, and roll back
  • Supports parallel stages, conditions, and approvals
  • Survives a Jenkins restart and can resume

Cons

  • Slightly steeper learning curve (you need to learn the syntax)
  • A small typo in the Jenkinsfile can break the build

Freestyle vs Declarative Pipeline: Side-by-Side

Feature Freestyle Job Declarative Pipeline
Configuration Web UI (clicks) Code (Jenkinsfile)
Stored in Git No Yes
Learning curve Very easy Moderate
Multi-stage workflows Difficult Built in
Stage visualization No Yes (Stage View)
Parallel execution Limited Yes
Reusability Low High
Best for Simple jobs, learning Real CI/CD projects

When Should You Use Which?

Use a Freestyle Job when:

  • You are a beginner running your first Jenkins lab
  • The task is small (one script, a quick test, a cleanup job)
  • You just want to understand how Jenkins works

Use a Declarative Pipeline when:

  • You are building a real CI/CD workflow (build → test → push → deploy)
  • You want your pipeline stored in GitHub with your code
  • You work in a team or want a production-style setup
  • You plan to integrate tools like Docker, SonarQube, ECR, or Kubernetes

How to Create a Pipeline Job on Jenkins (EC2)

  1. Open Jenkins at http://:8080
  2. Click New Item, enter a name, and select Pipeline
  3. Under Pipeline, choose Pipeline script from SCM
  4. Select Git and paste your repository URL
  5. Set the branch (for example main) and the Script Path as Jenkinsfile
  6. Click Save, then Build Now
  7. Open Stage View to watch each stage run

Tip: Make sure port 8080 is open in your EC2 Security Group, and store secrets such as Docker Hub credentials in Manage Jenkins → Credentials, never inside the Jenkinsfile.

My Recommendation

Start with a Freestyle job to understand the basics: how Jenkins pulls code, runs a shell command, and shows console output. Once you are comfortable, move to Declarative Pipelines. They are the industry standard for CI/CD, they are cleaner, and they make your project look far more professional on your GitHub and resume.

Conclusion

Freestyle jobs are great for learning, but Declarative Pipelines are what you will use in real projects. Treating your pipeline as code gives you version control, visibility, and repeatability, which are the core ideas of DevOps on AWS.

If you are learning Jenkins on EC2 too, try converting one of your Freestyle jobs into a Jenkinsfile today. It is the best way to learn.

title: Upgrade Evidence for Packages: Helping AI Agents Patch Safely
summary:
AI agents now open dependency upgrades faster than most engineering teams can review them. Safe patching is not just about bumping a version, it is about proving the bump held.

According to Sonatype's 2026 State of the Software Supply Chain report, 27.76% of 36,870 AI-generated upgrade recommendations pointed to versions that do not exist in any registry.

This ai agent package upgrade evidence guide breaks down why unverified upgrades fail and what proof every change should carry. It also shows how to record that proof in your pipeline.

You will see where human approval belongs, so your team can let agents patch with confidence and keep a clean, reviewable audit trail for every dependency change.

Why Do AI Agent Dependency Upgrades Fail Without Evidence?

Transitive dependencies change what nobody reviewed

An agent that bumps one direct package rarely changes just one package. The new version can pull in a dozen transitive dependencies, and each carries its own code, maintainers, and risks.

Reviewers usually read the manifest diff, yet the real change lives in the lockfile. Public data does not fill the gap either. Sonatype's analysis found that nearly 65% of open source CVEs lacked an NVD-assigned CVSS score.

Therefore, severity labels alone cannot tell an agent which upgrade is safe, or tell a reviewer why it was chosen.

A green build is not proof of a safe upgrade

A passing build only shows that the code compiles and the tests you wrote still pass. It does not show that the version exists in the registry. It also cannot show that the version is free of known flaws, or that the changed code paths were exercised.

Moreover, an agent explains its choice in fluent text, which feels like evidence but is not. Without a stored record of what was checked, nobody can reconstruct the decision later.

For software supply chain security reviews, that missing record is the real failure, not the bad version itself.

What Is AI Agent Package Upgrade Evidence?

AI agent package upgrade evidence is the verifiable record that proves an automated dependency change was necessary, correct, tested, and approved.

Detection tools stop at the alert, so AI agent package upgrade evidence has to be produced by the step that actually changes the code.

Think of it as a commit-level receipt. Each upgrade carries six items, and a reviewer should be able to answer every question without opening a terminal.

Together they form a package upgrade audit trail that survives staff changes and audit cycles. Notice that the registry check sits next to the test results.

The first confirms the package is real, while the second confirms your application still behaves.

How to Build an Upgrade Evidence Record Step by Step

Reliable ai agent package upgrade evidence starts in the pipeline, so the pipeline below treats evidence as a build artifact. If the file is missing or incomplete, the merge fails.

Capture the dependency diff before and after

Snapshot the lockfile before the agent runs, then diff it afterward. Record every direct and transitive change, not only the package the agent targeted.

Next, confirm each new version exists in the registry, since models can name releases that were never published. A simple lookup such as npm view handles this for npm packages, and the result belongs in the record.

Store the advisory ID that triggered the change as well, so the reason for the upgrade travels with the code. Repeat this for every ecosystem in the repository, because mixed stacks hide gaps.

Attach regression testing results to the change

Run automated dependency upgrade testing against the new dependency tree and store the report with the change ID.

Regression testing should cover the code paths that import the upgraded package, not just the overall pass rate.

If any test fails, the agent either repairs the code or abandons the upgrade, and the record should show which happened. Keep the report as a build artifact so auditors can open it months later. No passing tests means no evidence, and no evidence means no merge.

A minimal evidence record looks like this:

{
  "change_id": "upg-0042",
  "package": "lodash",
  "ecosystem": "npm",
  "from": "4.17.15",
  "to": "4.17.21",
  "advisory_ids": ["CVE-2021-23337"],
  "transitive_changes": 0,
  "registry_verified": true,
  "tests": { "suite": "regression", "passed": 187, "failed": 0 },
  "approval": { "tier": "patch", "approved_by": "reviewer@example.com" },
  "rollback_ref": "git:9f3c2ab"
}

A CI gate can then fail closed:

- name: Verify upgrade evidence
  run: |
    npm view "lodash@$NEW_VERSION" version
    jq -e '.registry_verified == true and .tests.failed == 0 and .rollback_ref != null' "evidence/$CHANGE_ID.json"

Where Should Human Approval Sit in Safe Package Patching?

Not every upgrade deserves the same scrutiny. A practical human approval workflow ties review depth to the version change. Patch releases with complete evidence can auto-merge to staging after a spot check. Minor releases need one reviewer who reads the evidence pack. Major releases get a full review and a tested rollback plan.

Tool comparisons such as LibX vs Snyk vs Dependabot show that scanners handle detection well. Yet dependency security only improves when the fix is also tested and recorded.

Automated vulnerability remediation closes that loop by upgrading the package, generating the code change, testing it, and handing the reviewer an evidence pack.

As a result, the reviewer's job shifts from hunting for facts to approving them.

Package Upgrade Evidence Checklist for Engineering Teams

Use this checklist to judge whether your ai agent package upgrade evidence is strong enough before an agent merges anything.

Each item maps to a field in the evidence record, so the checklist doubles as a review template.

Teams that adopt even four of these items gain a defensible package upgrade audit trail for the next software supply chain security review.

  • Lockfile diff stored, including transitive dependencies.
  • Advisory ID linked to the reason for the change.
  • Registry lookup confirms the exact version exists.
  • Regression tests run and attached as an artifact.
  • Approval tier matches the version change.
  • Rollback reference points to a tested commit.
  • Evidence file required by the CI gate, with the build failing when it is missing.

Verified Upgrades Beat Fast Upgrades

Agents will keep proposing upgrades, and the teams that benefit most will be the ones that demand proof with every change.

Xccelera builds an AI security dependency upgrader and vulnerability auto-resolver. It finds vulnerable and outdated dependencies, upgrades them, remediates the affected code, and tests each fix before it ships.

Every scan, upgrade, and fix is recorded as evidence, and human approval stays in the loop where your policies require it. That combination turns agent speed into something engineering leaders can trust and auditors can verify.

If your backlog of security upgrades keeps growing faster than your review capacity, start by asking what evidence each patch leaves behind.

title: What Does a Production Incident Actually Cost? A Practical Way to Calculate It
summary:
A production incident is rarely just a few minutes of downtime.

An API starts failing. An alert fires. Engineers join a Slack channel, open dashboards, inspect logs, follow traces, check recent deployments and start trying to understand what changed.

Eventually, the issue gets resolved.

But how much did that incident actually cost?

Most engineering teams track uptime, error rates and Mean Time to Resolution (MTTR). Far fewer calculate the engineering time consumed by incidents and translate it into a financial number.

That number can make a big difference when prioritizing reliability improvements.

1. Start with the engineering cost

The easiest place to start is the time engineers spend investigating and resolving incidents.

You need four inputs:

  • Number of incidents per month
  • Average resolution time per incident
  • Average number of engineers involved
  • Loaded hourly cost per engineer

The formula is:

Monthly engineering incident cost =

Incidents per month × Hours per incident × Engineers involved × Cost per engineer-hour

Let's use an example.

Assume an engineering team experiences:

Input Value
Incidents per month 8
Average resolution time 3 hours
Engineers involved 3
Loaded engineer-hour cost $75

The calculation:

8 × 3 × 3 × $75 = $5,400/month

That's $64,800 annually in engineering time.

This is not necessarily what the company loses in revenue. It is the estimated cost of engineering capacity spent handling production incidents.

2. Engineering time is only one part of the cost

A complete incident-cost analysis should distinguish between several categories.

Engineering time

The direct cost of engineers investigating, mitigating, fixing and validating an incident.

Customer impact

Customers may experience failed requests, interrupted workflows, degraded performance or loss of access to important features.

Revenue impact

For transaction-heavy products, failed payments, abandoned checkouts and interrupted business workflows can have measurable financial consequences.

Support and recovery

Support teams may spend additional time responding to tickets, communicating with customers and processing service credits or refunds.

Opportunity cost

Time spent repeatedly investigating incidents is time engineers cannot spend building features, improving architecture or addressing technical debt.

These costs should be calculated separately wherever possible. Otherwise, it's easy to count the same impact twice.

3. Why investigation time matters

MTTR is often discussed as one number, but the incident lifecycle has several stages:

  1. Detection – How long does it take to recognize the problem?
  2. Investigation – How long does it take to understand the cause?
  3. Remediation – How long does it take to implement and validate the fix?

A significant part of engineering effort can disappear into investigation.

Why?

Because information is fragmented.

An engineer might have to move between an error tracker, a log explorer, a distributed tracing system, a session replay tool and Git history.

They then manually correlate timestamps, trace IDs, affected requests and recent deployments.

The problem isn't always a lack of telemetry. It's the time required to connect the available evidence.

4. How to reduce the cost

Reducing incident cost doesn't necessarily mean preventing every failure. It also means making failures faster to understand and resolve.

Some practical improvements:

Correlate observability signals.

Make it possible to move from an error to its relevant logs, traces and request context without manually searching across systems.

Connect incidents to deployments and code changes.

Understanding what changed recently can help narrow down the investigation.

Improve incident context.

Group recurring errors, identify affected services and make relevant evidence available from the beginning.

Reduce repetitive investigation.

Use automation and AI-assisted analysis to gather evidence and suggest likely root causes.

Keep remediation reviewable.
