title: I ranked 7 Android cloud services by one question: will the device still be the same device in three months?
summary:
Disclosure first: I work with DuoPlus, on the growth side. So yes, it's on this list, and yes, it's near the top. I'll tell you where it falls short too, and I checked every other product's claims against its own website this week instead of going from memory.

Why this list exists: most cloud phone and device cloud roundups rank by "how many devices" or "how cheap." That's not what breaks for the teams I talk to. They're small QA shops, two-person dev teams, agencies looking after a dozen client apps. The question that actually costs them time is boring: when I open this Android environment next month, is it still logged in, still configured, still mine? Or am I starting from zero again?

So that's the ranking criterion. Fit for small dev/QA teams and agencies that need stable, isolated Android environments that last. Not gaming, and not one-off test runs (though some tools below are great at those).

1. DuoPlus

https://www.duoplus.net/share/market

DuoPlus gives you real ARM Android cloud phones, on Android 10, 11, 12 and 15. Each one is an isolated, independent device environment with its own data and login state, and it stays a fixed, long-term environment, so the phone you set up for a client in March is the same phone in June.

The part agencies care about is handover. You can share a device with a teammate in one click and they pick it up already logged in. When someone goes on leave, nobody spends an afternoon re-entering passwords and waiting on 2FA codes from the client.

Other things I actually use: per-device proxy and region settings, local environments in 150+ countries/regions, bulk install/uninstall/launch of apps across a batch of devices, root, and an API. Billing is per-minute. There are browser, desktop and mobile clients. There are also cloud numbers, which I use for testing our own app's signup and OTP flows without passing someone's personal SIM around the office.

Fits: agencies holding client app accounts long-term, small QA teams that want persistent devices they can hand to each other, anyone doing regional checks.

Drawbacks, honestly: it's Android only, so if your release checklist includes iOS you need a second tool. And it's not a test-automation grid with built-in reporting. If what you want is "upload APK, run Espresso suite on 40 device models, get a video per failure," the next three entries do that better.

2. Genymotion SaaS

https://www.genymotion.com/

Genymotion is the one I'd point a pure dev team at. Their site lists Genymotion SaaS ("optimized for team work, CI/CD and agentic AI"), a PaaS version on AWS, Alibaba, GCP and Azure, and Genymotion Desktop for PC and Mac. Integrations they name: Detox, GitHub Actions, CircleCI, Bitrise, Jenkins.

These are Android virtual devices built to be spun up from a pipeline, and they also pitch browser-based support and demo use.

Fits: dev teams that want Android devices wired into CI, plus support teams that need to reproduce a customer's bug from a browser tab.

Less ideal when: you need one specific device to hold a client's logged-in state for months and get passed between people. That's not what a CI emulator is shaped for.

3. AWS Device Farm

https://aws.amazon.com/device-farm/

Real physical phones and tablets hosted by AWS. You can run automated tests (Appium, Espresso, Calabash, or their built-in suite with no scripting), do manual remote sessions, and get videos, logs and performance data back. You can set location, language and network conditions.

The interesting bit for this list: their private device lab option gives you iOS and Android devices for your exclusive use and, per their page, lets you persist settings between sessions. That gets much closer to "my device stays my device."

Fits: teams already on AWS who need real hardware coverage, including iOS, hooked into Jenkins or Android Studio.

Less ideal when: you're a five-person agency without anyone who wants to own AWS config. And the shared pool is built for test runs, not long-lived logged-in accounts.

4. BrowserStack App Live

https://www.browserstack.com/app-live

BrowserStack says 30,000+ real iOS and Android devices. You can upload dev APK/AAB/IPA builds or install production apps from the stores, debug with logs and crash reports, and test on up to four devices at once. Their Custom Device Lab adds exclusive device access with options like app persistence and SIM binding.

Fits: QA teams who need wide model coverage across iOS and Android, fast.

Less ideal when: the job is keeping a handful of long-term environments for ongoing client work. You'd be paying for breadth you don't use, and persistence lives in the custom lab tier, not the default.

5. GeeLark

https://www.geelark.com/

GeeLark offers ARM-based cloud phones for Android apps plus multi-account browser profiles for web, both in one workspace. Team features are solid on paper: team members can be added free, roles and permissions, operation logs, groups/tags/notes for organising profiles. They also mention MCP so you can connect an AI agent to manage the phones and profiles, and they list GPS/SIM simulation across 150+ countries.

Fits: social and marketing teams who want phones and browser profiles managed side by side, with scheduling and AI content tools on top.

Less ideal when: you're a dev/QA team. A big chunk of the product is about posting, content generation and engagement automation, which you'll pay attention to (and maybe pay for) without needing.

6. VMOSCloud

https://www.vmoscloud.com/

VMOSCloud runs Android cloud phones with a strong lean toward social media automation: an AI workflow feature that turns text prompts into actions, a Synchronizer that mirrors one device's actions across many, and a Team Hub with roles and permissions. Their homepage lists Google Play Integrity, SafetyNet and Widevine L1. "App Test" appears in their industry list, though most of the page is about growing social accounts.

Fits: operators running many social accounts who want synchronized control.

Less ideal when: you want a dev-first tool. I'd also read their data policy closely if you plan long-term use: their FAQ says data is automatically deleted once the subscription ends, which is fine, just plan exports around it.

7. Redfinger

https://www.cloudemulator.net/

One of the older names. Redfinger has Android, Windows, web and iOS access, a Redfinger for Business line, and servers in the US, Taiwan and Singapore. Their site mentions device simulation for testing alongside gaming and cross-border marketing.

Fits: individuals and small teams who want a simple cloud Android device on several platforms.

Less ideal when: you need team handover and region coverage beyond those three server locations.

Honourable mentions: LDCloud and UgPhone

Both are positioned mainly for gaming. LDCloud (https://www.ldcloud.net/) leads with 24/7 AFK play, multi-instance and sync operation. UgPhone (https://www.ugphone.com/) lists tiers on Android 10, 12 and 13 with servers in places like Hong Kong, Germany, Japan, the USA and Singapore. For client QA work, I wouldn't start here.

How I'd actually choose

If I'm honest, the decision usually comes down to one question. Is the device disposable (run tests, throw away) or durable (holds state, gets handed between people for months)?

Disposable: Genymotion, AWS Device Farm, BrowserStack. Pick by whether you need iOS and how much CI you already have.

Durable: that's where DuoPlus, GeeLark, VMOSCloud and Redfinger sit, and I'd rank them by how painless handover and regional setup are for a non-engineer on your team. That's why DuoPlus is first on my list.

Plenty of teams end up with one of each. What hurts is using a disposable tool for durable work and wondering why everyone keeps logging in again.

If you've ranked these differently for your own team, I'd like to hear why in the comments, especially if you run client work on BrowserStack's custom lab.

title: BIGF v2.4 Lab: Enforcing Deterministic AI Agent Boundaries with OPA, Rego & RFC 8785
summary:
Welcome to the **VITI Labs* hands-on guide.*

System prompts are not security boundaries. If an autonomous AI agent is allowed to delegate tasks to sub-agents (Agent-to-Agent / A2A) or execute financial and infrastructure mutations, governance must happen outside the LLM at a deterministic runtime gate.

In this lab, you will build and test a complete Business Impact Governance Framework (BIGF v2.4) policy gate using Open Policy Agent (OPA), Rego, and RFC 8785 JSON Canonicalization (JCS).

Architecture: How the Gate Works

Every A2A delegation or actuation request passes through three deterministic stages before execution:

  1. Ingress Sanitization (BIGF-DCS): Raw JSON floats (IEEE 754) are rejected immediately (422 Unprocessable). All currency and threshold values must be encoded as 10-4 fixed-point strings ("2450.5000").
  2. Cryptographic Lineage (RFC 8785 JCS + SHA-256): The child contract must carry the exact SHA-256 hash of its canonicalized parent contract (parent_jcs_sha256) to prevent privilege injection or chain tampering.
  3. Monotonic Narrowing (B × S × T): A child agent can never expand its parent's authority:
    • B-Axis (Business Impact): child.max_exposure_fp4 <= parent.max_exposure_fp4 and currencies must match.
    • S-Axis (Situational State / BIII): child.min_biii_fp4 >= parent.min_biii_fp4 (integrity requirements can only tighten), and live telemetry BIII must meet the threshold.
    • T-Axis (Time & Telemetry): child.max_ttl_sec <= parent.max_ttl_sec, and the contract must fall strictly within the parent's [iat, exp] window.

Step 1: Project Structure

Create a directory bigf-opa-lab with four files:

bigf-opa-lab/
├── jcs_hash.py        # RFC 8785 canonicalizer & SHA-256 lineage generator
├── bigf_gate.rego     # Deterministic BIGF v2.4 OPA policy
├── bigf_gate_test.rego# Runnable OPA unit test suite (200 OK, 403 Halt, 422 Reject)
└── input_valid.json   # Sample A2A parent-to-child delegation payload

Step 2: RFC 8785 Canonicalizer (jcs_hash.py)

Before OPA evaluates a delegation chain, the orchestrator or ingress proxy canonicalizes the parent contract per RFC 8785 (sorted keys, zero insignificant whitespace, UTF-8) and verifies parent_jcs_sha256.

import hashlib
import json

def canonicalize_jcs(obj: dict) -> bytes:
    """RFC 8785 deterministic JSON canonicalization (UTF-8)."""
    return json.dumps(
        obj,
        sort_keys=True,
        separators=(",", ":"),
        ensure_ascii=False
    ).encode("utf-8")

def compute_jcs_sha256(obj: dict) -> str:
    """Computes the deterministic SHA-256 lineage hash."""
    return hashlib.sha256(canonicalize_jcs(obj)).hexdigest()

if __name__ == "__main__":
    parent_contract = {
        "bigf_version": "2.4.0",
        "contract_id": "a2a-parent-9f8e7d6c",
        "delegation_depth": 1,
        "exp": 1794509100,
        "iat": 1794508800,
        "invariants": {
            "b_axis": {
                "currency": "EUR",
                "max_exposure_fp4": "10000.0000",
                "regulatory_anchor": ["DORA", "NIS2"]
            },
            "s_axis": {
                "allowed_transitions": ["INVOICE_VERIFY", "SETTLEMENT_EXECUTE"],
                "min_biii_fp4": "0.8000"
            },
            "t_axis": {
                "max_ttl_sec": 300
            }
        },
        "iss": "ed25519:3b6a27bcceb6a42d62a3a8d02a6f0d73653215771de243a63ac048a18b59da29",
        "parent_jcs_sha256": None,
        "sub": "agent:procurement-eu-01"
    }
    print("parent_jcs_sha256:", compute_jcs_sha256(parent_contract))

Step 3: The Deterministic Rego Gate (bigf_gate.rego)

Save this policy as bigf_gate.rego. Notice how Rego enforces fail-closed physics: if any violation fires, allow defaults to false and the gate emits a structured 403 HARD HALT or 422 REJECTED decision record.

package bigf.v2_4.gate

import rego.v1

# Fail-closed default
default allow := false

# 1. BIGF-DCS Ingress Guard: Reject any raw JSON floating-point numbers
dcs_float_violations contains msg if {
    some path, val in walk(input)
    is_number(val)
    # In JSON/Rego, non-integers (e.g., 2450.5) fail exact integer division check
    round(val) != val
    msg := sprintf("422 BIGF-DCS Type Violation: IEEE 754 float detected at %v", [path])
}

# Fixed-point string parser (10^-4 scaling via to_number on validated strings)
parse_fp4(str) := num if {
    is_string(str)
    regex.match(`^\d+\.\d{4}$`, str)
    num := to_number(str)
}

# 2. Cryptographic Lineage & Depth Checks
violations contains "CRYPTO_AXIS: parent_jcs_sha256 mismatch" if {
    input.child.parent_jcs_sha256 != input.computed_parent_jcs_sha256
}

violations contains "CRYPTO_AXIS: Invalid delegation depth increment" if {
    input.child.delegation_depth != input.parent.delegation_depth + 1
}

# 3. B-Axis (Business Impact Monotonic Narrowing)
violations contains "B_AXIS: Currency mismatch between parent and child" if {
    input.child.invariants.b_axis.currency != input.parent.invariants.b_axis.currency
}

violations contains "B_AXIS: Child exposure exceeds parent ceiling" if {
    child_exp := parse_fp4(input.child.invariants.b_axis.max_exposure_fp4)
    parent_exp := parse_fp4(input.parent.invariants.b_axis.max_exposure_fp4)
    child_exp > parent_exp
}

violations contains "B_AXIS: Requested action amount exceeds child ceiling" if {
    req_amt := parse_fp4(input.request.amount_fp4)
    child_exp := parse_fp4(input.child.invariants.b_axis.max_exposure_fp4)
    req_amt > child_exp
}

# 4. S-Axis (Situational Integrity & Transition Subset)
violations contains "S_AXIS: Child weakened min_biii_fp4 requirement" if {
    child_biii := parse_fp4(input.child.invariants.s_axis.min_biii_fp4)
    parent_biii := parse_fp4(input.parent.invariants.s_axis.min_biii_fp4)
    child_biii < parent_biii
}

violations contains "S_AXIS: Live telemetry BIII below required threshold" if {
    live_biii := parse_fp4(input.telemetry.live_biii_fp4)
    req_biii := parse_fp4(input.child.invariants.s_axis.min_biii_fp4)
    live_biii < req_biii
}

violations contains "S_AXIS: Requested transition not permitted by child contract" if {
    not input.request.transition in input.child.invariants.s_axis.allowed_transitions
}

violations contains "S_AXIS: Child transitions exceed parent scope" if {
    some t in input.child.invariants.s_axis.allowed_transitions
    not t in input.parent.invariants.s_axis.allowed_transitions
}

# 5. T-Axis (Time Window & TTL Bounds)
violations contains "T_AXIS: Child TTL exceeds parent max_ttl_sec" if {
    input.child.invariants.t_axis.max_ttl_sec > input.parent.invariants.t_axis.max_ttl_sec
}

violations contains "T_AXIS: Child validity window escapes parent [iat, exp]" if {
    input.child.iat < input.parent.iat
}

violations contains "T_AXIS: Child expiration exceeds parent expiration" if {
    input.child.exp > input.parent.exp
}

violations contains "T_AXIS: Contract expired at evaluation timestamp" if {
    input.telemetry.now_utc > input.child.exp
}

# Final Deterministic Gate Decision
allow if {
    count(dcs_float_violations) == 0
    count(violations) == 0
}

# Canonical Decision Record (CDR) Output
decision := {
    "status": "422 UNPROCESSABLE",
    "state": "INGRESS_SCHEMA_VIOLATION",
    "privileges_propagated": 0,
    "violations": dcs_float_violations,
} if {
    count(dcs_float_violations) > 0
} else := {
    "status": "403 HARD HALT",
    "state": "UNVERIFIED_CRITICAL_STATE",
    "privileges_propagated": 0,
    "violations": violations,
} if {
    count(violations) > 0
} else := {
    "status": "200 OK",
    "state": "VERIFIED_EXECUTION",
    "approved_amount_fp4": input.request.amount_fp4,
    "biii_fp4": input.telemetry.live_biii_fp4,

event_model_payload.summary:
Welcome to the **VITI Labs* hands-on guide.*

System prompts are not security boundaries. If an autonomous AI agent is allowed to delegate tasks to sub-agents (Agent-to-Agent / A2A) or execute financial and infrastructure mutations, governance must happen outside the LLM at a deterministic runtime gate.

In this lab, you will build and test a complete Business Impact Governance Framework (BIGF v2.4) policy gate using Open Policy Agent (OPA), Rego, and RFC 8785 JSON Canonicalization (JCS).

Architecture: How the Gate Works

Every A2A delegation or actuation request passes through three deterministic stages before execution:

  1. Ingress Sanitization (BIGF-DCS): Raw JSON floats (IEEE 754) are rejected immediately (422 Unprocessable). All currency and threshold values must be encoded as 10-4 fixed-point strings ("2450.5000").
  2. Cryptographic Lineage (RFC 8785 JCS + SHA-256): The child contract must carry the exact SHA-256 hash of its canonicalized parent contract (parent_jcs_sha256) to prevent privilege injection or chain tampering.
  3. Monotonic Narrowing (B × S × T): A child agent can never expand its parent's authority:
    • B-Axis (Business Impact): child.max_exposure_fp4 <= parent.max_exposure_fp4 and currencies must match.
    • S-Axis (Situational State / BIII): child.min_biii_fp4 >= parent.min_biii_fp4 (integrity requirements can only tighten), and live telemetry BIII must meet the threshold.
    • T-Axis (Time & Telemetry): child.max_ttl_sec <= parent.max_ttl_sec, and the contract must fall strictly within the parent's [iat, exp] window.

Step 1: Project Structure

Create a directory bigf-opa-lab with four files:

bigf-opa-lab/
├── jcs_hash.py        # RFC 8785 canonicalizer & SHA-256 lineage generator
├── bigf_gate.rego     # Deterministic BIGF v2.4 OPA policy
├── bigf_gate_test.rego# Runnable OPA unit test suite (200 OK, 403 Halt, 422 Reject)
└── input_valid.json   # Sample A2A parent-to-child delegation payload

Step 2: RFC 8785 Canonicalizer (jcs_hash.py)

Before OPA evaluates a delegation chain, the orchestrator or ingress proxy canonicalizes the parent contract per RFC 8785 (sorted keys, zero insignificant whitespace, UTF-8) and verifies parent_jcs_sha256.

import hashlib
import json

def canonicalize_jcs(obj: dict) -> bytes:
    """RFC 8785 deterministic JSON canonicalization (UTF-8)."""
    return json.dumps(
        obj,
        sort_keys=True,
        separators=(",", ":"),
        ensure_ascii=False
    ).encode("utf-8")

def compute_jcs_sha256(obj: dict) -> str:
    """Computes the deterministic SHA-256 lineage hash."""
    return hashlib.sha256(canonicalize_jcs(obj)).hexdigest()

        "bigf_version": "2.4.0",
        "contract_id": "a2a-parent-9f8e7d6c",

Step 3: The Deterministic Rego Gate (bigf_gate.rego)

Save this policy as bigf_gate.rego. Notice how Rego enforces fail-closed physics: if any violation fires, allow defaults to false and the gate emits a structured 403 HARD HALT or 422 REJECTED decision record.

package bigf.v2_4.gate

import rego.v1

# Fail-closed default
default allow := false

# 1. BIGF-DCS Ingress Guard: Reject any raw JSON floating-point numbers
dcs_float_violations contains msg if {
    some path, val in walk(input)
    is_number(val)
    # In JSON/Rego, non-integers (e.g., 2450.5) fail exact integer division check
    round(val) != val
    msg := sprintf("422 BIGF-DCS Type Violation: IEEE 754 float detected at %v", [path])
}

# Fixed-point string parser (10^-4 scaling via to_number on validated strings)
parse_fp4(str) := num if {
    is_string(str)
    regex.match(`^\d+\.\d{4}$`, str)
    num := to_number(str)
}

# 2. Cryptographic Lineage & Depth Checks
violations contains "CRYPTO_AXIS: parent_jcs_sha256 mismatch" if {
    input.child.parent_jcs_sha256 != input.computed_parent_jcs_sha256
}

violations contains "CRYPTO_AXIS: Invalid delegation depth increment" if {
    input.child.delegation_depth != input.parent.delegation_depth + 1
}

# 3. B-Axis (Business Impact Monotonic Narrowing)
violations contains "B_AXIS: Currency mismatch between parent and child" if {
    input.child.invariants.b_axis.currency != input.parent.invariants.b_axis.currency
}

violations contains "B_AXIS: Child exposure exceeds parent ceiling" if {
    child_exp := parse_fp4(input.child.invariants.b_axis.max_exposure_fp4)
    parent_exp := parse_fp4(input.parent.invariants.b_axis.max_exposure_fp4)
    child_exp > parent_exp
}

violations contains "B_AXIS: Requested action amount exceeds child ceiling" if {
    req_amt := parse_fp4(input.request.amount_fp4)
    child_exp := parse_fp4(input.child.invariants.b_axis.max_exposure_fp4)
    req_amt > child_exp
}

# 4. S-Axis (Situational Integrity & Transition Subset)
violations contains "S_AXIS: Child weakened min_biii_fp4 requirement" if {
    child_biii := parse_fp4(input.child.invariants.s_axis.min_biii_fp4)
    parent_biii := parse_fp4(input.parent.invariants.s_axis.min_biii_fp4)
    child_biii < parent_biii
}

violations contains "S_AXIS: Live telemetry BIII below required threshold" if {
    live_biii := parse_fp4(input.telemetry.live_biii_fp4)
    req_biii := parse_fp4(input.child.invariants.s_axis.min_biii_fp4)
    live_biii < req_biii
}

violations contains "S_AXIS: Requested transition not permitted by child contract" if {
    not input.request.transition in input.child.invariants.s_axis.allowed_transitions
}

violations contains "S_AXIS: Child transitions exceed parent scope" if {
    some t in input.child.invariants.s_axis.allowed_transitions
    not t in input.parent.invariants.s_axis.allowed_transitions
}

# 5. T-Axis (Time Window & TTL Bounds)
violations contains "T_AXIS: Child TTL exceeds parent max_ttl_sec" if {
    input.child.invariants.t_axis.max_ttl_sec > input.parent.invariants.t_axis.max_ttl_sec
}

violations contains "T_AXIS: Child validity window escapes parent [iat, exp]" if {
    input.child.iat < input.parent.iat
}

violations contains "T_AXIS: Child expiration exceeds parent expiration" if {
    input.child.exp > input.parent.exp
}

violations contains "T_AXIS: Contract expired at evaluation timestamp" if {
    input.telemetry.now_utc > input.child.exp
}

# Final Deterministic Gate Decision
allow if {
    count(dcs_float_violations) == 0
    count(violations) == 0
}

# Canonical Decision Record (CDR) Output
decision := {
    "status": "422 UNPROCESSABLE",
    "state": "INGRESS_SCHEMA_VIOLATION",
    "privileges_propagated": 0,
    "violations": dcs_float_violations,
} if {
    count(dcs_float_violations) > 0
} else := {
    "status": "403 HARD HALT",
    "state": "UNVERIFIED_CRITICAL_STATE",
    "privileges_propagated": 0,
    "violations": violations,
} if {
    count(violations) > 0
} else := {
    "status": "200 OK",
    "state": "VERIFIED_EXECUTION",
    "approved_amount_fp4": input.request.amount_fp4,
    "biii_fp4": input.telemetry.live_biii_fp4,
    "lineage_sha256": input.child.parent_jcs_sha256,
}

title: Pi-hole on Kubernetes with PowerDNS and external-dns
summary:
A home or office network needs two things from its DNS. Devices should
find the services that run in the network by name, such as
pihole.home.example. Ads and trackers should not resolve at all. Pi-hole
does the second part. It answers with 0.0.0.0 for every domain on its
deny list and blocklists, and forwards the rest. The names of the local
services belong in a zone that a server holds with authority. PowerDNS
Authoritative Server holds that zone here, and external-dns writes a
record into it for every Kubernetes Service that asks for a name.

This post puts the three together from three
recipes that kadet-hub publishes for
Kapitan. The project is
pihole-powerdns
in kadet-hub/examples. Its check script deploys it to a new
kind cluster on every change and once a week, and fails
when a step below stops working. All names are under .example, which
RFC 2606 reserves, so none of them belongs to a real domain.

What each recipe brings

A recipe is a directory of Kapitan classes, published as a signed OCI
artifact. All three render with the kubernetes
generator 1.14.0.

  • pihole 1.0.0 runs Pi-hole 2026.10.1, rebuilt from the Docker Compose example of docker-pi-hole. It renders a StatefulSet with a 1Gi claim for /etc/pihole and a Service with DNS on port 53 over UDP and TCP and the web interface on ports 80 and 443.
  • powerdns 1.0.0 runs PowerDNS Authoritative Server 5.1.5 with its zones in SQLite on a 1Gi claim. An init container creates the zone that applications.powerdns.zone names. The HTTP API listens on port 8081 and takes the key from a Secret.
  • external-dns-powerdns 1.0.0 runs external-dns 0.23.0, rebuilt from the external-dns project's Helm chart 1.23.0. It includes powerdns and writes into its zone through the API.

The fetch inventory

Kapitan 0.36.3 reads the inventory before it
fetches dependencies, so a recipe cannot be fetched by the inventory that
uses it. The recipes are pinned in a separate fetch inventory,
fetch/targets/recipes.yml:

parameters:
  kapitan:
    dependencies:
      - type: oci
        source: ghcr.io/kadet-hub/recipes/pihole:1.0.0@sha256:09ded1b7816cc669ecc45b539fc349c9cace2a53b1c23962561c7b3c3589746c
        output_path: inventory/classes/recipes/pihole
      - type: oci
        source: ghcr.io/kadet-hub/recipes/external-dns-powerdns:1.0.0@sha256:5e497b87ee50d7027666310355f5e12bb850c0d67f7e6a1d5ec2249843219fb3
        output_path: inventory/classes/recipes/external-dns-powerdns
      - type: oci
        source: ghcr.io/kadet-hub/recipes/powerdns:1.0.0@sha256:5330189e01e87845dd0dbaae1270929b566f1e62f0591502b07d69ed68e92fda
        output_path: inventory/classes/recipes/powerdns

Version and digest come from the signed
index, downloaded and verified as in the next
section. A recipe's index record also lists the recipes it includes:

jq -c '.recipes["external-dns-powerdns"]["1.0.0"].includes[] | [.name, .version]' index.json

["powerdns","1.0.0"]

Every recipe unpacks into inventory/classes/recipes/, so the
project can hold one version of powerdns. It has to be the one that
external-dns-powerdns includes. The index also lists powerdns 1.0.1,
whose readiness probe connects to the API port instead of the DNS port.
That version fits this project once an external-dns-powerdns version that
includes it is published.

Verify, then pull by digest

The registry's
consumer docs
give the steps, and check runs them for all three recipes. For pihole:

id=https://github.com/kadet-hub/registry/.github/workflows/release.yml@refs/heads/main
gh release download --repo kadet-hub/registry --pattern 'index.json*'
gh attestation verify index.json --bundle index.json.sigstore.json --owner kadet-hub --cert-identity "$id"
d=sha256:09ded1b7816cc669ecc45b539fc349c9cace2a53b1c23962561c7b3c3589746c
tmp=$(mktemp -d)
gh attestation verify "oci://ghcr.io/kadet-hub/recipes/pihole@$d" --owner kadet-hub --cert-identity "$id"
oras pull -o "$tmp" "ghcr.io/kadet-hub/recipes/pihole@$d"
mkdir -p inventory/classes/recipes/pihole
tar -xf "$tmp/pihole.tar" -C inventory/classes/recipes/pihole --no-same-owner

The first attestation check proves that the
registry's release workflow signed the index. The second proves the same
for the recipe. check also requires the index to list 1.0.0 under
pihole with that digest and yanked: null. The recipes pin the
kubernetes generator by digest, and check verifies and pulls it into
lib/kubernetes the same way. Kapitan then compiles without --fetch,
which checks neither digests nor attestations.

One zone, two targets

The zone is set once, in the class inventory/classes/home.yml:

parameters:
  home:
    zone: home.example

The target dns renders PowerDNS and external-dns
into the namespace dns. inventory/targets/dns.yml:

classes:
  - home
  - recipes.external-dns-powerdns
parameters:
  namespace: dns
  kapitan:
    vars:
      target: dns
  applications:
    powerdns:
      api_key: ?{base64:dns/powerdns-api-key||random:str:40}
      zone: ${home.zone}

applications.powerdns.zone names the zone that PowerDNS creates at its
first start. external-dns-powerdns uses the same value as its
--domain-filter, so external-dns writes only names in that zone. The
API key is a ref. The first compile creates a random
value of 40 characters and stores it under refs/dns/powerdns-api-key.
The base64 backend only encodes, so use one that encrypts, such as gpg or
Vault, for an install that matters.

The target pihole renders Pi-hole into the namespace pihole.
inventory/targets/pihole.yml:

classes:
  - home
  - recipes.pihole
parameters:
  namespace: pihole
  kapitan:
    vars:
      target: pihole
  applications:
    pihole:
      password: ?{base64:pihole/password||random:str:32}
  components:
    pihole:
      env:
        # kind's cluster DNS. On a LAN this is the resolver Pi-hole forwards to.
        FTLCONF_dns_upstreams: kube-dns.kube-system.svc.cluster.local
        # The home zone goes to PowerDNS. FTL's dnsmasq resolves the name of
        # the Service once, when FTL starts.
        FTLCONF_misc_dnsmasq_lines: server=/${home.zone}/powerdns.dns.svc.cluster.local
      service:
        annotations:
          # external-dns writes this name into the zone.
          external-dns.kubernetes.io/hostname: pihole.${home.zone}

Pi-hole 6 accepts each setting of its pihole.toml as an environment
variable named FTLCONF_

_. The recipe passes
components.pihole.env through, so the wiring needs no change to the
recipe.

misc.dnsmasq_lines adds lines to the configuration of dnsmasq, the DNS
server inside FTL, Pi-hole's core. The line
server=/home.example/powerdns.dns.svc.cluster.local sends every query
for the zone and its subdomains to PowerDNS. Every other name goes to the
servers in dns.upstreams. dnsmasq accepts a host name in server= and
resolves it when it reads its configuration (parse_server in
src/dnsmasq/option.c of FTL v6.8). The Service powerdns must
therefore exist when Pi-hole starts. If the Service is deleted and
created again with a new cluster IP, Pi-hole needs a restart.

Pi-hole's own setting for this is conditional forwarding,
dns.revServers. It writes the same server= line, but each entry also
requires the network range of a reverse zone and sends the PTR queries
for that range to the same server. PowerDNS holds no reverse zone here,
so misc.dnsmasq_lines carries only the forward zone.

The annotation on the Service pihole asks external-dns for the name
pihole.home.example. The recipe runs external-dns with
--publish-internal-services, so the record holds the Service's cluster
IP. Any Service in any namespace gets a record the same way.

Compile and deploy

The recipes are written for the omegaconf inventory backend. With
Kapitan 0.36.3 and its omegaconf extra installed as the consumer docs
describe:

printf 'global:\n  inventory-backend: omegaconf\n' > .kapitan
kapitan compile
kapitan compile --reveal

The first compile creates the refs. The second writes their values into
the Secrets. The compile renders 10 files for dns, two of them the
CRDs of external-dns's chart, and 3 for pihole.

kubectl create namespace dns
kubectl label namespace dns pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce=restricted
kubectl apply -R -f compiled/dns
kubectl -n dns rollout status statefulset/powerdns
kubectl create namespace pihole
kubectl label namespace pihole pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce=baseline
kubectl apply -R -f compiled/pihole

find the services that run in the network by name, such as

record into it for every Kubernetes Service that asks for a name.

This post puts the three together from three
recipes that kadet-hub publishes for
Kapitan. The project is

title: Terraform for Beginners: Build Cloud Infrastructure by Writing Simple Code
summary:
A short story to start

Imagine you spent a whole afternoon clicking around the Azure or AWS website to set up a server, a network, a database and a few security rules. It works. Well done.

Now your manager says: "Great, can you build exactly the same thing again for testing, and another copy in Europe?" Can you remember every click? Every setting? Every small box you ticked?

Most people cannot. That is the problem Terraform solves. Instead of clicking, you write down what you want in a simple text file. Terraform reads the file and builds it for you, the same way, every time.

1. What is Terraform, in one sentence?

Terraform is a tool that turns a simple text file into real cloud infrastructure.

This idea is called Infrastructure as Code, or IaC for short. Your servers, networks and databases are described in code, just like an app.

A good way to picture it is a building plan. An architect does not build a house by shouting instructions to workers one by one. She draws a plan. Builders follow the plan. If you want ten identical houses, you use the same plan ten times. Terraform files are your plan.

Terraform is made by a company called HashiCorp. It works with almost every cloud: AWS, Microsoft Azure, Google Cloud and hundreds of other services. You may also hear about OpenTofu, a free open source version that works in almost the same way. Everything you learn here applies to both.

2. How does Terraform work?


Figure 1: You write the code, Terraform reads it, the provider talks to the cloud.

There are only a few moving parts:

  1. You write files ending in .tf that describe what you want.
  2. Terraform reads those files and works out what needs to be created, changed or deleted.
  3. A provider is a plugin that knows how to talk to one platform. There is a provider for AWS, one for Azure, one for Google Cloud, and many more. Think of it as a translator.
  4. The real cloud ends up with the servers, networks and storage you asked for.

The most important idea: you describe what you want, not how to build it step by step. Terraform works out the steps.

3. The words you will hear (made simple)

Word What it means in plain English
Provider The plugin that talks to a platform, such as aws or azurerm.
Resource One thing you want to create, such as a server, a network or a storage bucket.
Variable A value you can change without editing the main code, such as a region or a name.
Output A value Terraform prints at the end, such as a website address or a server IP.
State Terraform's memory of what it has already built.
Plan A preview of the changes Terraform is about to make.
Module A reusable bundle of Terraform code, like a Lego set you can use again and again.

4. Install Terraform

Go to the official Terraform website from HashiCorp, download the version for your computer (Windows, Mac or Linux) and follow the install steps. On a Mac you can also use Homebrew, and on Windows you can use Chocolatey or winget.

Then open a terminal and type:

terraform -version

If you see a version number, you are ready. I also recommend installing Visual Studio Code with the official HashiCorp Terraform extension. It colours your code and spots mistakes as you type.

5. Your first project (no cloud account needed)

The best way to learn Terraform without any risk of a cloud bill is to start with something local. We will ask Terraform to create a simple text file on your own computer. The steps are exactly the same as for a real server in the cloud.

Step 1: Create a folder and a file

Make a new folder called my-first-terraform and inside it create a file called main.tf with this code:

resource "local_file" "hello" {
  filename = "hello.txt"
  content  = "Hello from Terraform!"
}

Let us read it slowly:

  • resource says "I want to create something".
  • "local_file" is the type of thing: a file on this computer.
  • "hello" is the nickname we give it inside our code.
  • Inside the curly brackets are the settings: the file name and what to write in it.

Step 2: Run the four magic commands


Figure 2: init, plan, apply and destroy. You will use these every single day.

Open a terminal in your folder and run:

terraform init

init gets everything ready. It notices you used local_file and downloads the provider that knows how to create files.

terraform plan

plan shows a preview. You should see something like "Plan: 1 to add, 0 to change, 0 to destroy". Nothing has been created yet. This is your chance to check before anything happens.

terraform apply

apply does the real work. Terraform shows the plan again and asks you to type yes. Type it and press Enter. Now look in your folder: there is a new file called hello.txt with your message inside. You just used Infrastructure as Code.

Step 3: Make a change

Change the content line to say "Hello again from Terraform!" and run terraform plan. Terraform notices the difference and tells you it will replace the file. Run terraform apply, type yes, and open the file again. It has been updated. You did not tell Terraform how to update it. You only changed what you wanted.

Step 4: Clean up 

terraform destroy

destroy deletes everything Terraform created in this folder. Type yes and hello.txt disappears. In the real cloud this is your best friend: one command and everything you built for practice is gone, so you are not paying for it.

6. The state file: Terraform's memory


Figure 3: Terraform compares what you want, what it remembers and what really exists.

After you ran apply, you may have noticed a new file called terraform.tfstate. This is Terraform's memory. It records what Terraform has built, so next time it knows what already exists and what needs to change.

A few simple rules for the state file:

  • Never edit it by hand. Let Terraform manage it.
  • Never share it publicly or upload it to GitHub. It can contain passwords and private details.
  • In a team, store it in a shared, safe place such as an Azure Storage account, an AWS S3 bucket or HCP Terraform. This is called remote state, and it stops two people changing the same thing at the same time.

7. Variables and outputs: making your code flexible

Hard coding values works, but variables let you reuse the same code for different situations. Add this to your main.tf:

variable "message" {
  default = "Hello from Terraform!"
}

resource "local_file" "hello" {
  filename = "hello.txt"
  content  = var.message
}

output "file_name" {
  value = local_file.hello.filename
}
  • The variable block creates a value called message with a default.
  • var.message uses that value inside the resource.
  • The output block prints the file name when apply finishes.

Now you can change the message without touching the resource, for example: terraform apply -var="message=Good morning".

8. A small real cloud example

When you are ready for the cloud, the pattern is exactly the same. Here is how you would create a storage bucket on AWS:

provider "aws" {
  region = "eu-west-1"
}

resource "aws_s3_bucket" "my_bucket" {
  bucket = "my-first-terraform-bucket-12345"
}

Same commands: init, plan, apply. Same clean up: destroy. Before you try it, create a free tier account, set a budget alert, and log in with the AWS command line tool so Terraform can use your account. Bucket names must be unique across the whole world, so change the numbers at the end.

9. Good habits from day one

  1. Always read the plan before you type yes. It tells you exactly what will be created, changed or deleted.
  2. Keep your .tf files in Git, so you have a history of every change.
  3. Add a .gitignore file that keeps out terraform.tfstate, the .terraform folder and any files with secrets.
  4. Run terraform fmt to tidy your code and terraform validate to catch mistakes early.
  5. Make small changes and apply often, instead of one giant change.
  6. Destroy practice resources as soon as you finish, so you do not get a surprise bill.

10. Common beginner mistakes

  • Typing yes without reading the plan, and deleting something important.
  • Uploading the state file or secret keys to a public GitHub repository.
  • Changing things by hand in the cloud website after Terraform built them. Terraform will get confused, or undo your changes next time.
  • Forgetting to run terraform init after adding a new provider.
  • Trying to learn modules, workspaces and remote state on day one. Master the basics first.

11. A simple learning path

Stage What to do
Week 1 Install Terraform and complete the local_file project in this guide.
Week 2 Learn variables, outputs and terraform fmt and validate.
Week 3 Create one small real cloud resource, then destroy it.
Week 4 Build a small network and a virtual machine, and keep your code on GitHub.
After that Learn remote state, modules, and running Terraform inside a CI/CD pipeline.

Final words

Terraform can look scary at first, but the core idea is simple: write down what you want, check the plan, then let Terraform build it. The same file can build the same setup again tomorrow, next month or in another country.

Your challenge this week: create the hello.txt file with Terraform, change it, and destroy it. Those three commands, plan, apply and destroy, are the heart of everything you will ever do with Terraform.

Happy building!

Imagine you spent a whole afternoon clicking around the Azure or AWS website to set up a server, a network, a database and a few security rules. It works. Well done.

Now your manager says: "Great, can you build exactly the same thing again for testing, and another copy in Europe?" Can you remember every click? Every setting? Every small box you ticked?

Most people cannot. That is the problem Terraform solves. Instead of clicking, you write down what you want in a simple text file. Terraform reads the file and builds it for you, the same way, every time.

1. What is Terraform, in one sentence?

Terraform is a tool that turns a simple text file into real cloud infrastructure.

This idea is called Infrastructure as Code, or IaC for short. Your servers, networks and databases are described in code, just like an app.

A good way to picture it is a building plan. An architect does not build a house by shouting instructions to workers one by one. She draws a plan. Builders follow the plan. If you want ten identical houses, you use the same plan ten times. Terraform files are your plan.

Terraform is made by a company called HashiCorp. It works with almost every cloud: AWS, Microsoft Azure, Google Cloud and hundreds of other services. You may also hear about OpenTofu, a free open source version that works in almost the same way. Everything you learn here applies to both.

2. How does Terraform work?


Figure 1: You write the code, Terraform reads it, the provider talks to the cloud.

There are only a few moving parts:

  1. You write files ending in .tf that describe what you want.
  2. Terraform reads those files and works out what needs to be created, changed or deleted.
  3. A provider is a plugin that knows how to talk to one platform. There is a provider for AWS, one for Azure, one for Google Cloud, and many more. Think of it as a translator.
  4. The real cloud ends up with the servers, networks and storage you asked for.

The most important idea: you describe what you want, not how to build it step by step. Terraform works out the steps.

3. The words you will hear (made simple)

Word What it means in plain English
Provider The plugin that talks to a platform, such as aws or azurerm.
Resource One thing you want to create, such as a server, a network or a storage bucket.
Variable A value you can change without editing the main code, such as a region or a name.
Output A value Terraform prints at the end, such as a website address or a server IP.
State Terraform's memory of what it has already built.
Plan A preview of the changes Terraform is about to make.
Module A reusable bundle of Terraform code, like a Lego set you can use again and again.

4. Install Terraform

Go to the official Terraform website from HashiCorp, download the version for your computer (Windows, Mac or Linux) and follow the install steps. On a Mac you can also use Homebrew, and on Windows you can use Chocolatey or winget.

Then open a terminal and type:

terraform -version

If you see a version number, you are ready. I also recommend installing Visual Studio Code with the official HashiCorp Terraform extension. It colours your code and spots mistakes as you type.

5. Your first project (no cloud account needed)

The best way to learn Terraform without any risk of a cloud bill is to start with something local. We will ask Terraform to create a simple text file on your own computer. The steps are exactly the same as for a real server in the cloud.

Step 1: Create a folder and a file

Make a new folder called my-first-terraform and inside it create a file called main.tf with this code:

resource "local_file" "hello" {
  filename = "hello.txt"
  content  = "Hello from Terraform!"
}

Let us read it slowly:

  • resource says "I want to create something".
  • "local_file" is the type of thing: a file on this computer.
  • "hello" is the nickname we give it inside our code.
  • Inside the curly brackets are the settings: the file name and what to write in it.

Step 2: Run the four magic commands


Figure 2: init, plan, apply and destroy. You will use these every single day.

Open a terminal in your folder and run:

terraform init

init gets everything ready. It notices you used local_file and downloads the provider that knows how to create files.

terraform plan

plan shows a preview. You should see something like "Plan: 1 to add, 0 to change, 0 to destroy". Nothing has been created yet. This is your chance to check before anything happens.

terraform apply

apply does the real work. Terraform shows the plan again and asks you to type yes. Type it and press Enter. Now look in your folder: there is a new file called hello.txt with your message inside. You just used Infrastructure as Code.

Step 3: Make a change

Change the content line to say "Hello again from Terraform!" and run terraform plan. Terraform notices the difference and tells you it will replace the file. Run terraform apply, type yes, and open the file again. It has been updated. You did not tell Terraform how to update it. You only changed what you wanted.

Step 4: Clean up 

terraform destroy

destroy deletes everything Terraform created in this folder. Type yes and hello.txt disappears. In the real cloud this is your best friend: one command and everything you built for practice is gone, so you are not paying for it.

6. The state file: Terraform's memory


Figure 3: Terraform compares what you want, what it remembers and what really exists.

After you ran apply, you may have noticed a new file called terraform.tfstate. This is Terraform's memory. It records what Terraform has built, so next time it knows what already exists and what needs to change.

A few simple rules for the state file:

  • Never edit it by hand. Let Terraform manage it.
  • Never share it publicly or upload it to GitHub. It can contain passwords and private details.
  • In a team, store it in a shared, safe place such as an Azure Storage account, an AWS S3 bucket or HCP Terraform. This is called remote state, and it stops two people changing the same thing at the same time.

7. Variables and outputs: making your code flexible

Hard coding values works, but variables let you reuse the same code for different situations. Add this to your main.tf:

variable "message" {
  default = "Hello from Terraform!"
}

resource "local_file" "hello" {
  filename = "hello.txt"
  content  = var.message
}

output "file_name" {
  value = local_file.hello.filename
}
  • The variable block creates a value called message with a default.
  • var.message uses that value inside the resource.
  • The output block prints the file name when apply finishes.

Now you can change the message without touching the resource, for example: terraform apply -var="message=Good morning".

8. A small real cloud example

When you are ready for the cloud, the pattern is exactly the same. Here is how you would create a storage bucket on AWS:

provider "aws" {
  region = "eu-west-1"
}

resource "aws_s3_bucket" "my_bucket" {
  bucket = "my-first-terraform-bucket-12345"
}

Same commands: init, plan, apply. Same clean up: destroy. Before you try it, create a free tier account, set a budget alert, and log in with the AWS command line tool so Terraform can use your account. Bucket names must be unique across the whole world, so change the numbers at the end.

9. Good habits from day one

  1. Always read the plan before you type yes. It tells you exactly what will be created, changed or deleted.
  2. Keep your .tf files in Git, so you have a history of every change.
  3. Add a .gitignore file that keeps out terraform.tfstate, the .terraform folder and any files with secrets.
  4. Run terraform fmt to tidy your code and terraform validate to catch mistakes early.
  5. Make small changes and apply often, instead of one giant change.
  6. Destroy practice resources as soon as you finish, so you do not get a surprise bill.

10. Common beginner mistakes

  • Typing yes without reading the plan, and deleting something important.
  • Uploading the state file or secret keys to a public GitHub repository.
  • Changing things by hand in the cloud website after Terraform built them. Terraform will get confused, or undo your changes next time.
  • Forgetting to run terraform init after adding a new provider.
  • Trying to learn modules, workspaces and remote state on day one. Master the basics first.

11. A simple learning path

Stage What to do
Week 1 Install Terraform and complete the local_file project in this guide.
Week 2 Learn variables, outputs and terraform fmt and validate.
Week 3 Create one small real cloud resource, then destroy it.
Week 4 Build a small network and a virtual machine, and keep your code on GitHub.
After that Learn remote state, modules, and running Terraform inside a CI/CD pipeline.

Final words

Terraform can look scary at first, but the core idea is simple: write down what you want, check the plan, then let Terraform build it. The same file can build the same setup again tomorrow, next month or in another country.

Your challenge this week: create the hello.txt file with Terraform, change it, and destroy it. Those three commands, plan, apply and destroy, are the heart of everything you will ever do with Terraform.

Happy building!

title: CI/CD for Beginners: A Simple Guide to Shipping Code Without Stress
summary:
A short story to start

It is Friday evening. A developer has just finished a new feature. To put it live, he logs in to the server, copies some files across, restarts the app and goes home. On Saturday morning the phone rings. The website is down. He forgot one small file.

This story has happened in thousands of companies. Not because people are careless, but because people are human. We get tired, we rush, we forget steps.

CI/CD is the cure for this problem. It hands the boring, repeatable work to a robot that never gets tired and never forgets a step. In this guide I will explain it in plain words, show you some simple pictures, and walk you through your very first pipeline.

1. What is CI/CD, in one sentence?

CI/CD is a robot that builds, tests and delivers your code automatically every time you make a change.

That is really all it is. The letters stand for two ideas that work together:

  • CI means Continuous Integration.
  • CD means Continuous Delivery (and sometimes Continuous Deployment).

Let us look at each one.

CI: Continuous Integration

"Integration" simply means joining your code with everybody else's code. "Continuous" means doing it all the time, in small pieces, instead of once in a while in one big painful merge.

Each time someone pushes code, the CI robot:

  1. Grabs the newest code.
  2. Builds it (puts the app together).
  3. Runs the tests (checks that nothing is broken).
  4. Reports back with a green tick (all good) or a red cross (something broke).

Think of a bakery. Every loaf is checked before it leaves the kitchen. If one comes out burnt, you find out straight away, not when a customer complains.

CD: Continuous Delivery and Continuous Deployment

Once the code has passed all the checks, CD takes over and gets it ready to go live.

  • Continuous Delivery: the code is always packaged and ready to release. A person still presses the final "go live" button.
  • Continuous Deployment: there is no button. If all the tests pass, the code goes live by itself.

Most beginners and most companies start with Continuous Delivery. You keep a human in control of the last step until you trust your tests.


Figure 1: A simple pipeline. You write and push. The robot builds, tests and delivers.

2. Why should you care?

Here is the honest difference CI/CD makes in day to day work:


Figure 2: The same team, before and after CI/CD.

  • Fewer mistakes. The robot follows the same steps in the same order every time.
  • Faster feedback. You find out a change is broken in minutes, while you still remember what you changed.
  • Less fear. When releasing is easy and safe, teams release small changes often instead of big risky ones.
  • More time for real work. Nobody spends their evening copying files to a server.

This is also why almost every DevOps, cloud or software job advert today mentions CI/CD. It is a basic skill, like knowing how to use Git.

3. The words you will hear (made simple)

Word What it means in plain English
Pipeline The full list of automatic steps, from your code to the live app.
Trigger The event that starts the pipeline, for example pushing code or opening a pull request.
Job A group of steps that run together on one machine, for example "build and test".
Step One single action, like "install Python" or "run the tests".
Runner The computer that does the work. Often a fresh cloud machine that is thrown away afterwards.
Artifact The finished package the pipeline produces, like a zip file or a Docker image.
Environment A place your app runs, for example test, staging or production (the real live site).
Secret A password or key the pipeline needs, stored safely and hidden from logs.

4. Popular CI/CD tools

There are many tools, but they all do the same basic job. Here are the ones you will meet most often:

  • GitHub Actions: built into GitHub. Free for public projects and the easiest place to start.
  • GitLab CI/CD: built into GitLab, very popular in companies that use GitLab.
  • Jenkins: the old, trusted, open source workhorse. You run it on your own server.
  • Azure DevOps Pipelines: Microsoft's tool, common in companies that use Azure.
  • CircleCI and others: hosted services that connect to your code.

My advice: start with GitHub Actions. You probably already have a GitHub account, there is nothing to install, and what you learn carries over to every other tool.

5. Build your first pipeline with GitHub Actions

Let us build a real pipeline. It will run your tests every time you push code. You only need a GitHub account.


Figure 3: A trigger starts a workflow. A workflow has jobs. A job has steps.

Step 1: Make a tiny project

Create a new repository on GitHub and add two small Python files.

A file called calculator.py:

def add(a, b):
    return a + b

And a test file called test_calculator.py:

from calculator import add

def test_add():
    assert add(2, 3) == 5

The test simply checks that 2 plus 3 really gives 5.

Step 2: Add the pipeline file

In your repository, create this folder and file: .github/workflows/ci.yml. GitHub looks in that exact folder for pipelines. Put this inside:

name: My first pipeline

on: [push]

jobs:
  build-and-test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-python@v5
        with:
          python-version: "3.12"
      - run: pip install pytest
      - run: pytest

Step 3: Understand it line by line

  • name: the name you will see on GitHub.
  • on: [push]: the trigger. Run this every time someone pushes code.
  • jobs / build-and-test: one job with a name we chose.
  • runs-on: ubuntu-latest: GitHub gives us a fresh Linux machine for free.
  • actions/checkout: step one, download our code onto that machine.
  • actions/setup-python: step two, install Python.
  • pip install pytest: step three, install the testing tool.
  • pytest: step four, run the tests.

YAML files care about spaces. Use two spaces for each level and never use the Tab key. Most beginner errors come from wrong spacing.

Step 4: Push and watch

Commit and push the files. Open your repository on GitHub and click the Actions tab. You will see your pipeline running. After a minute or so you should see a green tick. Congratulations, you just built a CI pipeline.

Step 5: Break it on purpose

This is the fun part. Change the add function so it returns a - b instead of a + b, then push again. The pipeline will run, the test will fail and you will see a red cross. Click it and read the error. This is exactly what CI is for: it caught the mistake before anyone else saw it.

Fix the code, push again, and watch it turn green.

Step 6: Adding the CD part later

When you are ready, you add a second job called deploy that only runs if the tests pass. It might upload your app to a cloud service such as Azure App Service, AWS or a simple static website host. The idea is always the same: tests first, deploy second, and only if the tests were green.

6. Good habits from day one

  1. Push small changes often. Small changes are easy to test and easy to fix.
  2. Keep your pipeline fast. If it takes an hour, people stop waiting for it. Aim for minutes.
  3. Never write passwords in the YAML file. Use GitHub Secrets (Settings, then Secrets and variables) and the pipeline can read them safely.
  4. Protect your main branch. Set a rule that code can only be merged when the pipeline is green.
  5. Write tests. A pipeline with no tests is like a smoke alarm with no battery. It looks nice but protects nothing.
  6. Fix red pipelines first. A broken pipeline that everyone ignores is worse than no pipeline.

7. Common beginner mistakes

  • Putting the workflow file in the wrong folder. It must be .github/workflows/.
  • Mixing tabs and spaces in YAML.
  • Deploying straight to the live site before you trust your tests.
  • Copying a huge pipeline from the internet without understanding it. Start small and grow it one step at a time.
  • Leaving secrets in the code "just for testing". Bots search public repositories for leaked keys all day long.

8. A simple learning path

Stage What to do
Week 1 Learn basic Git: commit, push, branch and pull request.
Week 2 Build the GitHub Actions pipeline from this guide and break it on purpose.
Week 3 Add tests to a small project of your own and run them in the pipeline.
Week 4 Add a deploy job that publishes a simple website to the cloud.
After that Learn Docker images in pipelines, environments with approvals, and try Jenkins or Azure DevOps.

Final words

CI/CD sounds like a big technical word, but the idea is simple: let a robot do the boring checks every single time, so humans can focus on building good things.

Your challenge this week: build the small pipeline from this guide, watch it turn green, then break it and watch it turn red. Once you see that red cross catch your own mistake, you will never want to work without CI/CD again.

Happy building!

title: How to Deploy GLM-4.5-Air with SGLang on a Dedicated GPU Server
summary:
Running a large language model on dedicated hardware gives you full control over the serving environment, model configuration and API access. In this guide, we deploy GLM-4.5-Air-FP8 from Z.ai on an NVIDIA GPU server using SGLang, exposing an OpenAI-compatible API.

This is a condensed version. The complete tutorial is on Leo Servers.

About the model

GLM-4.5-Air is a mixture-of-experts (MoE) model built for reasoning, coding and agent tasks. It has about 106B total parameters and about 12B active during inference. We use the FP8 checkpoint:

zai-org/GLM-4.5-Air-FP8

Hardware

Z.ai documents these NVIDIA configurations for GLM-4.5-Air-FP8:

Use case GPUs
Standard FP8 inference 2x H100
Full 128K context 4x H100

The full-featured conditions also call for more than 1TB of system RAM, a batch size of eight or less, and no CPU offloading. Treat these as a reference, not a universal minimum.

Prepare Ubuntu and verify the GPUs 

sudo apt update && sudo apt upgrade -y
sudo apt install -y curl git wget build-essential
ubuntu-drivers devices
sudo ubuntu-drivers install
sudo reboot

After the reboot:

nvidia-smi
nvidia-smi -L
nvidia-smi topo -m

Install SGLang 

curl -LsSf https://astral.sh/uv/install.sh | sh
source "$HOME/.local/bin/env"
mkdir -p ~/glm-deployment && cd ~/glm-deployment
uv venv --python 3.12
source .venv/bin/activate
uv pip install --prerelease=allow sglang

Point the Hugging Face cache at a large volume:

sudo install -d -o "$USER" -g "$(id -gn)" /data/huggingface
echo 'export HF_HOME=/data/huggingface' >> ~/.bashrc
source ~/.bashrc

Launch the model 

python -m sglang.launch_server \
    --model-path zai-org/GLM-4.5-Air-FP8 \
    --served-model-name glm-4.5-air-fp8 \
    --host 127.0.0.1 \
    --port 30000

Binding to 127.0.0.1 keeps the API off the public interface.

Test the API 

curl http://127.0.0.1:30000/v1/models

from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI(api_key="local-development", base_url="http://127.0.0.1:30000/v1")

response = client.chat.completions.create(
    model="glm-4.5-air-fp8",
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Explain the role of GPU memory in LLM inference."}],
    max_tokens=300,
)
print(response.choices[0].message.content)

Run it with systemd and secure it

A systemd unit keeps SGLang running and restarts it on failure. For remote access, use an authenticated HTTPS reverse proxy, firewall rules and private networking. Never expose an unauthenticated inference endpoint to the internet.

Read the full guide

The full tutorial includes the complete systemd unit file, monitoring tips and a troubleshooting table:

👉 How to Deploy Zhipu AI GLM-4.5-Air with SGLang on a Dedicated GPU Server

Z.ai documents these NVIDIA configurations for GLM-4.5-Air-FP8:

Use case GPUs
Standard FP8 inference 2x H100

The full-featured conditions also call for more than 1TB of system RAM, a batch size of eight or less, and no CPU offloading. Treat these as a reference, not a universal minimum.

Prepare Ubuntu and verify the GPUs 

sudo apt update && sudo apt upgrade -y
sudo apt install -y curl git wget build-essential
ubuntu-drivers devices
sudo ubuntu-drivers install
sudo reboot

After the reboot:

nvidia-smi
nvidia-smi -L
nvidia-smi topo -m

Install SGLang 

curl -LsSf https://astral.sh/uv/install.sh | sh
source "$HOME/.local/bin/env"
mkdir -p ~/glm-deployment && cd ~/glm-deployment
uv venv --python 3.12
source .venv/bin/activate
uv pip install --prerelease=allow sglang

Point the Hugging Face cache at a large volume:

sudo install -d -o "$USER" -g "$(id -gn)" /data/huggingface
echo 'export HF_HOME=/data/huggingface' >> ~/.bashrc
source ~/.bashrc

Launch the model 

python -m sglang.launch_server \
    --model-path zai-org/GLM-4.5-Air-FP8 \
    --served-model-name glm-4.5-air-fp8 \
    --host 127.0.0.1 \
    --port 30000

Binding to 127.0.0.1 keeps the API off the public interface.

Run it with systemd and secure it

A systemd unit keeps SGLang running and restarts it on failure. For remote access, use an authenticated HTTPS reverse proxy, firewall rules and private networking. Never expose an unauthenticated inference endpoint to the internet.
